crops.name: Cherry Tomato

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Cherry tomatoes want soil that drains well and is rich in organic matter. If water sits on top of your bed after rain or stays soggy for more than a day, drainage is a problem, soggy roots will rot even if the soil is otherwise good. The easiest fix for most soils is to work in 2 to 3 inches of compost before planting, which improves both drainage and fertility at once. Tomatoes are heavy feeders, so starting with rich soil means less fertilizing mid-season.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Cherry tomatoes perform best in well-drained loam or sandy loam with high organic matter content. Adequate drainage is non-negotiable, waterlogged roots invite both Pythium root rot and nutrient lockout even in otherwise fertile soil. Working in 2 to 3 inches of compost before planting addresses both texture and fertility in one amendment. Tomatoes are heavy feeders, and organically rich soil reduces the mid-season fertilizer burden considerably.

ph.note_beginner: Soil pH is a measure of acidity on a scale from 1 to 14, where 7 is neutral. Tomatoes need it between about 6.0 and 6.8, the slightly acidic range where the nutrients they need are most available. Soils in the interior West (Arizona, Nevada, Utah, Colorado) often run alkaline (above 7), which can cause nutrient problems even when fertilizer is applied; growers in those regions often need to add sulfur before planting. Eastern and Midwestern soils are often naturally in the right range, but a $10 soil test from your local extension office tells you for certain.
ph.note_seasoned: Tomatoes are particularly sensitive to pH because it governs the solubility of phosphorus, calcium, and magnesium, three nutrients they consume in large quantities. At pH below 5.5, manganese and aluminum become increasingly available at phytotoxic levels; blossom-end rot risk rises as calcium uptake is impaired. Above 7.0, iron and manganese deficiencies drive interveinal chlorosis on younger leaves. In the alkaline soils common across the interior West and alkaline-irrigation regions, growers routinely need to acidify before planting. Eastern soils often run naturally in the preferred range; Pacific Northwest soils vary widely by parent material.

3.notes: Short season: choose varieties under 60 days like Tumbler or Sweet 100. Use black plastic mulch to warm soil.
3.zone_notes: Zone 3 is short-season but well-suited to cherry tomatoes. Cherry types (55-65 day) ripen before first frost even in Z3a. Start seeds 6 weeks before last frost. Choose Sungold, Sweet 100, or Tumbler for reliable harvest.

fertilizer.notes_beginner: When you see the first flowers opening, switch fertilizers. Use a balanced or all-purpose fertilizer early in the season, then switch to a tomato-specific or high-potassium fertilizer once flowers appear. Too much nitrogen (the first number on the package) after flowering pushes the plant to grow more leaves instead of fruit.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Time to feed your tomatoes. Switch to a tomato fertilizer or high-potassium fertilizer now to keep the fruit coming.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Look for three numbers on the fertilizer bag: those are the NPK ratio (nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium). For fruiting tomatoes, you want the third number to be the highest: something like 5-10-10 or 8-32-16 works well.
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Switch from balanced to high-potassium feed at flowering. Too much nitrogen produces leafy plants with little fruit.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time to feed your tomatoes, use tomato fertilizer to keep fruit coming

companions.note_beginner: Most tomato companion advice is garden tradition rather than tested fact. The clearest exception is marigolds, which can cut down on root pests, but only when planted thickly as a cover crop a couple of months ahead, not scattered among the tomatoes. In practice: keep fennel away, keep tomatoes away from their relatives like potatoes and eggplant if disease has been a problem for you, and try nasturtiums as a trap for aphids if aphids gave you trouble in past seasons.
companions.note_seasoned: Cherry tomato companions are dominated by traditional lore with selective extension backing. The marigold/nematode connection is the best-documented pairing in this crop's companion set, effective as a dense pre-season cover crop, not as scattered concurrent interplanting. For most growers, the practical guidance is straightforward: avoid fennel, keep tomatoes away from other Solanaceae family members (potatoes, eggplant) if disease pressure is a concern in your region, and consider nasturtiums as an aphid trap crop if aphid pressure was a problem in past seasons.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Basil
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Long-established pairing; flavor-improvement claims are traditional. Basil's aromatic compounds may deter some pest insects, though not extension-documented for this specific pair, but widely practiced and low risk.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Flavor-improvement and pest-deterrence claims are classic companion-planting tradition. Not documented in peer-reviewed research or T1 extension literature for this specific pairing.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: A long-standing pairing. Many gardeners say basil improves tomato flavor and may keep some pests away. There is no hard proof for this exact pair, but it is widely done and harmless.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Marigolds
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: French marigolds suppress root-knot nematodes, most effectively as a dense cover crop planted 2+ months before tomatoes, not as concurrent interplanting. Extension-documented mechanism.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Iowa State University Extension and UF/IFAS ENY-056 document alpha-terthienyl release suppressing root-knot nematodes. Extension consensus: dense cover crop 2+ months pre-season is effective; scattered concurrent interplanting has minimal effect. Whitefly deterrence claims are traditional and not extension-supported.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: French marigolds can reduce root-knot pests in the soil, but only when planted thickly as a cover crop a couple of months before the tomatoes, not as a few plants tucked in alongside them.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Parsley
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Flowering umbellifers attract predatory wasps and beneficial insects; mechanism is documented in biological control literature though the specific parsley-tomato pairing is not directly extension-tested.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Umbellifers attracting parasitic wasps and beneficial insects is a documented biological control mechanism (UC IPM, Cornell). The specific parsley-tomato pairing benefit is inferential: the mechanism is real but pairing-specific evidence is thin.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: When parsley is left to flower, the blooms draw in helpful insects that prey on garden pests. The effect is well established in general, though this exact parsley and tomato pairing has not been tested directly.

good_seasoned.name: Carrots
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Carrots' deep taproot partitions the root zone differently from tomato's fibrous roots, theoretically reducing below-ground competition. This is a plausible root-zone partitioning inference, not an extension-tested pairing.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Root-zone partitioning between taprooted and fibrous-rooted crops is a real ecology concept. The specific carrot-tomato pairing benefit is a plausible inference that has not been directly studied in extension research.

good_seasoned.name: Borage
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Borage flowers attract pollinators over an extended bloom period; may also repel tomato hornworm (traditional claim). Pollinator attraction is biologically plausible; hornworm repellence is tradition.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Borage as pollinator attractor is plausible and consistent with floral-resource literature. The hornworm-repellence claim is traditional companion-planting lore without T1 extension backing.

good_seasoned.name: Nasturtiums
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Nasturtiums function as a trap crop for aphids: aphids preferentially colonize nasturtiums, drawing them away from tomatoes. UC IPM documents trap-crop use of nasturtiums in vegetable gardens.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap-crop principle is documented in IPM literature. UC IPM references nasturtiums as aphid attractors. The specific nasturtium-tomato trap-crop pairing is referenced in extension-adjacent IPM guidance; strongest evidence is for brassica pests, but aphid trap-crop mechanism applies broadly.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Fennel
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Fennel is broadly allelopathic and suppresses growth of many neighboring plants. Extension literature documents fennel as a poor companion for most vegetables; the specific tomato interaction is traditional but consistent with fennel's known allelopathic properties.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Fennel's allelopathic properties are real and documented, but the specific 'stunts tomatoes' claim is traditional rather than directly extension-tested for this pair.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Fennel releases substances that stunt the growth of many plants around it, so it is a poor neighbor for most vegetables. The trouble with tomatoes is traditional advice, but it fits fennel's known habit of holding back its neighbors.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Brassicas
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Both brassicas and tomatoes are heavy feeders; close interplanting creates real competition for nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. Not a toxic pairing, but productivity of both crops is reduced under competition.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Inter-plant competition for macronutrients between heavy feeders is a real agronomic concept. The specific brassica-tomato pair is traditional; the underlying competition mechanism is mechanistically sound.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Cabbage-family plants and tomatoes are both hungry feeders, so planting them close together makes them compete for the same nutrients. It is not harmful, but both crops produce less.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Corn
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Both crops host the tomato fruit worm / corn earworm (Helicoverpa zea, same species). Planting together creates a concentrated host reservoir that amplifies pest pressure on both crops.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: H. zea (tomato fruit worm = corn earworm) is documented on both tomato and corn in UC IPM and Cornell IPM literature. Shared-host concentration is a well-established IPM principle. Planting these crops together in a home garden concentrates the pest population.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Corn and tomatoes are fed on by the same caterpillar pest. Growing them side by side gives that pest more to feed on and builds up the pressure on both crops.

bad_seasoned.name: Potatoes
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Both are Solanaceae and share primary diseases (late blight, Phytophthora infestans; early blight, Alternaria solani) and several pests. Planting together creates a continuous host bridge that sustains inoculum across the season and into following years. Crop rotation separating Solanaceae is the standard extension recommendation for disease management.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Extension literature (UMN, Cornell, Clemson HGIC) documents shared disease and pest pressure within Solanaceae and recommends rotation to break disease cycles. The specific tomato-potato pairing as a disease-management risk is extension-backed.

bad_seasoned.name: Eggplant
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Same family (Solanaceae), shares Colorado potato beetle pressure and early blight. Interplanting concentrates beetle and disease pressure; separating Solanaceae crops, even within a season, reduces crossover pest load.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Colorado potato beetle and early blight are documented shared pests/pathogens across Solanaceae in extension IPM literature. The specific eggplant-tomato bad-companion claim follows from the well-documented within-family pest/disease sharing principle.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_beginner: Clusters of tiny soft green or black insects on the growing tips and the undersides of leaves, often so small they look like dots. The leaves may start to curl or feel sticky. You might see ants walking up the stems, as they farm aphids for the sweet liquid the aphids produce.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray the colonies directly with a strong jet of water from a hose. For persistent infestations, apply insecticidal soap or neem oil spray, making sure to coat the leaf undersides where the aphids cluster.
pests.prevention_beginner: Plant marigolds or nasturtiums near your tomatoes, as both attract beneficial insects that eat aphids. Avoid over-fertilizing with high-nitrogen fertilizer, which produces the soft new growth aphids prefer.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.cause_beginner: Tiny soft-bodied insects that cluster on stems and the undersides of leaves. Their numbers can build up very fast in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Tomato hornworm
pests.symptoms_beginner: Large sections of leaves or whole stems stripped overnight. Look for fat green caterpillars (up to 4 inches long) that blend almost perfectly into the stems, but they are easier to spot by looking for the black droppings on the leaves below.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Hand-pick and drop in soapy water, it sounds simple but it works well. If you spot any with small white oval capsules stuck to their backs, leave those ones; parasitic wasps have laid eggs on them and the wasps will do the work for you.
pests.prevention_beginner: Till or turn your soil in autumn to destroy overwintering pupae. Planting dill or fennel nearby attracts the predatory wasps that prey on hornworms.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Large green caterpillars (up to 4 inches) stripping foliage. Leaves disappear rapidly. Black droppings on leaves.
pests.cause_seasoned: Manduca quinquemaculata moth larvae. Mid to late summer pest.
pests.cause_beginner: Large green caterpillars, the larvae of a moth, that feed on leaves and stems. They show up mostly in mid to late summer.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick, they are well camouflaged but easy to remove. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) spray. If white cocoons visible on back, leave them, as parasitic wasps are doing the work.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Till soil in autumn to kill overwintering pupae. Plant dill and basil nearby to attract predatory wasps.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny round holes scattered across the leaves, especially on young plants and seedlings. If you approach the plant quickly you'll see tiny shiny black beetles jumping off the leaves: that's the flea beetle.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover seedlings with floating row cover until plants are a few inches tall and growing strongly. Diatomaceous earth dusted on and around the leaves can help; reapply after rain.
pests.prevention_beginner: Transplanting larger, more established plants rather than direct-sowing reduces flea beetle damage, since seedlings are most vulnerable.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny round shot-holes in leaves, especially on seedlings and young plants. Small shiny black beetles jump when disturbed.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple flea beetle species. Most active in spring on young plants.
pests.cause_beginner: Small dark beetles that jump like fleas when disturbed and chew tiny holes in leaves. They are most active in spring on young plants.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Use row covers on seedlings. Apply diatomaceous earth. Neem oil spray.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Delay transplanting until plants are large. Use transplants rather than seeds.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms_beginner: Leaves look dusty or stippled, with tiny yellow or tan dots covering the surface. In bad infestations you'll see fine webbing on the undersides of leaves. Leaves may look bronzed or dry at the edges. Mites thrive in hot, dry weather.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray the undersides of leaves with a strong jet of water every day for a week, which disrupts mite populations significantly. Follow up with neem oil or insecticidal soap applied to leaf undersides if the problem persists.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather; water-stressed plants are more vulnerable. Misting the leaves in the morning raises local humidity, which mites dislike.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine stippling or yellow dots on leaves. Fine webbing on leaf undersides. Leaves may bronze, dry out, and drop. Worst in hot dry weather.
pests.cause_seasoned: Tetranychus urticae and related species. Thrives in heat and drought.
pests.cause_beginner: Tiny mites, almost too small to see, that feed on leaves and leave fine specks or webbing. They thrive in hot, dry conditions.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast with water repeatedly. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap to leaf undersides. Increase humidity around plants.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather. Avoid dusty conditions. Introduce predatory mites.

diseases.name: Early blight
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Dark brown spots on the lower leaves, often with rings inside them like a target pattern. The leaves around the spots turn yellow, then the whole leaf dies and drops. The pattern starts at the bottom of the plant and moves upward.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove and throw away (do not compost) any affected leaves as soon as you spot them. Mulch the soil around the base of the plant to stop rain from splashing soil and fungal spores up onto the lower leaves.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Rotate your tomatoes, avoiding the same spot for at least 3 years. Water at the base of the plant rather than from overhead, and stake the plant to keep the foliage off the ground.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark brown spots with concentric rings on lower leaves first. Affected leaves yellow and drop. Spreads upward through plant.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Alternaria fungus. Favored by warm wet conditions.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that causes dark spots on the lower, older leaves first. It spreads in warm, wet weather, so keep the leaves as dry as you can.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves immediately. Apply copper-based fungicide preventively. Mulch soil to prevent splash-up.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate tomatoes every 3-4 years. Water at soil level. Space plants for airflow. Stake to keep foliage off ground.

diseases.name: Blossom end rot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Dark, sunken, leathery patches on the bottom of the fruit, the end where the flower was attached. It usually appears on the first fruits of the season. It is not contagious and doesn't spread between plants.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: The fix is consistent watering, not calcium supplements. Mulch around the base to help the soil hold moisture evenly, and water on a regular schedule rather than in big irregular bursts. Remove affected fruit; they won't recover.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Water consistently and deeply, as the most common trigger is irregular watering during fruit development. Avoid disturbing the roots by cultivating too close to the plant, and don't over-fertilize with nitrogen, which pushes the plant to grow faster than it can absorb calcium.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark, sunken, leathery patch at the bottom (blossom end) of fruit. Affects first fruits most. Not contagious.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Calcium deficiency in developing fruit, caused by irregular watering or root damage, not a pest or disease.
diseases.cause_beginner: A dark, sunken patch on the bottom of the fruit. It is not a pest or a disease: the fruit cannot get enough calcium, usually because watering has been uneven. Water steadily to prevent it.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Mulch to maintain even soil moisture. Water consistently. Foliar calcium spray provides some relief. Remove affected fruit.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Consistent watering is the key prevention. Avoid root disturbance. Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen.

diseases.name: Septoria leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small circular spots on the leaves, with tan or pale gray centers with dark brown borders, often with a faint yellow halo around the outside. They start on the lower leaves and move upward. Not as aggressive as early blight but disfiguring.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove affected leaves immediately. Apply copper-based fungicide if the problem is spreading. Improve airflow by staking or caging so leaves aren't touching each other.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Water at the soil level rather than overhead. Mulch to prevent soil splash. Rotate tomatoes to a different bed each year.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small circular spots with dark borders and pale gray centers, starting on lower leaves. Spots may have yellow halos.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Septoria lycopersici fungus. One of the most common tomato diseases.
diseases.cause_beginner: A common fungus that makes many small, round spots on the leaves. It spreads in wet conditions, so water at the soil and keep the leaves dry.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves. Apply copper fungicide. Ensure good air circulation.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate crops. Water at soil level. Mulch around plants.

diseases.name: Late blight
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Large, irregularly shaped brown patches that look water-soaked and spread fast, days not weeks. In humid weather you may see white fuzzy growth on the undersides of affected leaves. This one is serious; it can kill a healthy plant in a week.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove and destroy all affected plant material immediately, bag it and throw it in the trash, do not compost it. Apply copper-based fungicide preventively if you see it starting in your area and conditions are wet.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Choose disease-resistant varieties whenever possible. Stake for good airflow. Never leave tomato plant debris in the garden over winter, clear it all out at season's end.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Water-soaked, rapidly expanding brown patches on leaves and stems. White fuzzy growth on undersides in humid conditions. Can destroy plants in days.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Phytophthora infestans oomycete. The same pathogen that caused the Irish potato famine. Spreads rapidly in cool wet weather.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fast-moving disease that can collapse a plant within days in cool, wet weather. Remove and throw away affected plants right away so it does not spread.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy all affected material immediately, do not compost. Apply copper fungicide preventively in wet conditions.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant resistant varieties. Ensure excellent airflow. Never leave tomato debris in the garden over winter.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Every 2-3 days during hot weather, once a week when temperatures are cool. The difference is driven by evapotranspiration rate: at air temperatures above 80-85°F, plants lose water through leaves several times faster than at 60°F, so the soil dries proportionally faster. Container-grown plants dry out faster still and may need daily checking in peak summer heat.
watering.frequency_beginner: Every 2 to 3 days in hot weather, and about once a week when it is cool. Plants drink and lose much more water when it is hot, so the soil dries out faster. Plants in containers dry out even quicker and may need checking every day in peak summer heat.
watering.amount_seasoned: 1-2 inches of water per week total from rain plus irrigation. The goal is to wet the soil to 8-12 inches depth, deep enough to reach the main root mass and encourage roots to grow downward rather than staying near the surface. Light, shallow watering trains roots upward, making the plant more sensitive to heat and drought stress.
watering.amount_beginner: About 1 to 2 inches of water a week, counting rain and watering together. Water deeply enough to soak the soil down about 8 to 12 inches, where the main roots are. Deep watering pulls the roots downward, which makes the plant tougher in heat and dry spells; frequent shallow watering keeps the roots near the surface, where they dry out fast.
watering.method_seasoned: At soil level: soaker hose, drip line, or a hose placed at the base. Wet foliage is the primary route of entry for Septoria leaf spot, early blight, and late blight: fungal spores on the soil surface travel upward in splash water, and wet leaf surfaces give spores the moisture film they need to germinate and penetrate. Morning watering, if overhead watering is unavoidable, allows foliage to dry before evening, the most disease-permissive period.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the soil, not over the top of the plant: use a soaker hose, a drip line, or just hold the hose at the base. Wet leaves are how most tomato leaf diseases get started, so keeping the leaves dry is one of the best things you can do. If you do have to water from above, do it in the morning so the leaves dry off before evening.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Yellow lower leaves and cracked fruit are the two signs to watch for. Yellow leaves near the bottom of the plant mean the roots are sitting in waterlogged soil, and when the soil stays soggy, air gets squeezed out of it and the roots can't breathe. Cracked fruit usually follows a sudden heavy watering after the soil has been dry: the tomato swells fast and the skin splits. Both problems come from uneven watering, not just too much water overall.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Wilting during the day that bounces back overnight is the clearest sign your plant is thirsty: if it perks up after the sun goes down, water is the issue. If flowers drop before forming fruit, the plant may be under water stress: when it can't sustain fruit development, it sheds the flower at the stem (called abscission). Note that extreme heat above 90 degrees does the same thing, so blossom drop can happen even when you're watering regularly during a heat wave.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellow lower leaves, cracked fruit, persistently soggy soil. Yellowing lower leaves indicate roots are sitting in anaerobic (oxygen-depleted) conditions, as waterlogged soil displaces the air pores roots need to respire. Fruit cracking happens when a sudden surge of water causes rapid cell expansion in a fruit whose skin has already stopped stretching; common after heavy rain following a dry spell. Both are signs of inconsistency, not just total volume.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting leaves that recover overnight, blossom drop, dry cracked soil. Overnight recovery distinguishes water stress from heat stress or disease: if leaves perk up after the temperature drops, moisture is the limiting factor. Blossom drop under drought stress occurs because the plant triggers an abscission layer at the flower stem when it cannot sustain fruit development; high temperatures (above 90°F day / below 55°F night) cause the same response, so both stressors can operate simultaneously.

start_method.hardening_off_beginner: These plants were raised indoors and have never felt wind, direct sun, or cool nights. Hardening off means introducing them to outdoor life slowly over 7 to 10 days, starting with a few hours outside in a sheltered spot the first day, then more time and more sun each day. Skip this step and the plants will sulk for weeks after transplanting, or the leaves will scorch on the first sunny day. It is not optional for tomatoes.
start_method.notes_beginner: Start seeds indoors 6 to 8 weeks before your last frost date (look yours up if you don't know it, as it varies by 6 to 8 weeks across zones). When you transplant, dig a deeper hole than the pot and bury the stem right up to the lowest set of leaves, as new roots form all along the buried stem and make for a stronger, more drought-tolerant plant from the start.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost. Harden off over 7-10 days before transplanting. Transplant deep: bury stem up to lowest leaves to encourage roots.

container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: Deep preferred over wide; minimum 12-inch depth for adequate root development. Standard round 5- to 10-gallon nursery containers work well.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: A deep pot matters more than a wide one. Aim for at least 12 inches deep so the roots have room. A standard round 5 to 10 gallon pot works well.

drainage.saucer_practice_seasoned: Elevate container off saucer or remove standing water within an hour; saucers are useful for heat retention but roots should not sit in pooled water.
drainage.saucer_practice_beginner: Do not let the pot sit in a saucer of standing water. Lift the pot off the saucer, or empty the saucer within an hour of watering. A saucer is fine for keeping the pot warm, but the roots should never sit in pooled water.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Use a bag of potting mix made for containers. Do not use soil dug from the garden, which packs down too tightly and drains poorly in a pot.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: If your potting mix feels heavy or dense, mix in about 20% perlite, a lightweight volcanic material that keeps the mix from compacting around roots. Stir in a slow-release granular fertilizer at planting, following the label rate.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Incorporate 20-25% perlite by volume if the mix feels dense; add slow-release balanced fertilizer (e.g., 10-10-10 granular) at planting per label rate.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out much faster than garden beds, so in summer heat you may need to water every day. Stick your finger two inches into the soil; if it feels dry there, water thoroughly. Keeping moisture steady matters: letting the soil swing from bone-dry to soaked is the most common cause of blossom end rot (dark, sunken patches on the fruit bottom) in container tomatoes.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Potting mix can't hold onto nutrients the way garden soil does, so container tomatoes need regular feeding. Once your plant starts flowering, apply a balanced liquid fertilizer every one to two weeks. Alternatively, mix slow-release granules into the soil at planting and add one liquid feed mid-season. Don't skip this, as container plants run out of food faster than in-ground ones.
container_notes.notes_beginner: Cherry tomatoes do very well in pots. Use a 5-gallon pot at minimum, though a larger pot (10 gallons) holds moisture better and supports a bigger plant. Compact varieties like Tumbling Tom or Tiny Tim are designed for containers; full-size indeterminate cherry tomatoes will also work in 10-gallon containers with a sturdy cage. In hot weather, container plants dry out fast and may need water every day.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Excellent container crop. Use 5-10 gallon pots. Determinate or compact varieties (Tumbling Tom, Tiny Tim) are ideal. Water daily in heat.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry significantly faster than in-ground soil, so daily watering is often required during summer heat. Check moisture 2 inches below the surface daily. Consistent moisture is critical; irregular watering is a primary driver of blossom-end rot in containers.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Container medium has limited nutrient buffering capacity. Supplement with liquid balanced fertilizer every 1-2 weeks once flowering begins, or apply slow-release granular at planting plus a liquid mid-season boost. Containers are less forgiving of nutrient deficits than in-ground beds.

recommended: Tumbling Tom (compact-determinate, ideal for hanging baskets and containers)
Patio Choice (yellow, compact-determinate AAS winner, 18" plant)
varieties.note_beginner: Cherry tomatoes come in a few shapes: round, pear-shaped, and slightly larger elongated types called cocktail tomatoes. All are grown the same way. If you're not sure which to try, Sungold is a popular first choice with a sweet, complex flavor. Juliet is a common elongated type that holds up well on the vine.
varieties.note_seasoned: Cherry-class tomatoes include round cherry, pear-shaped, and cocktail (elongated cherry) types, cultivation is the same across all. Sungold is consistently rated the best-tasting cherry tomato by home gardeners worldwide. Juliet is the most common cocktail tomato.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes, all share blight and fusarium diseases
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not plant cherry tomatoes where you grew tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, or potatoes last year. These plants are all in the same family and share the same soil diseases, which can build up and carry over to the next crop.
rotation.note_beginner: Move your tomatoes to a different part of the garden each year, and don't come back to the same spot for at least 3 years. Soil diseases, including the wilts and blights that affect tomatoes, can survive in the soil or on old plant debris for multiple seasons. Rotation is the main tool home gardeners have to keep these in check. The same rule applies to peppers, eggplant, and potatoes: they share the same diseases, so avoid planting any of them where tomatoes grew recently.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate nightshades to a fresh bed every 3 years minimum. Soilborne pathogens, particularly Fusarium wilt (Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lycopersici), Verticillium wilt, and early blight (Alternaria solani), can persist in soil or on plant debris for multiple seasons. Fusarium and Verticillium are soil-systemic and resistant to most home-garden interventions once established; the primary management tool for the home gardener is rotation combined with resistant varieties. Avoid planting tomatoes after any Solanaceae crop (peppers, eggplant, potatoes), as these share the same pathogen suite.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: 1-2 weeks at room temperature (65-70°F). Ripe tomatoes held at room temperature continue producing small amounts of ethylene, which sustains flavor development. Stem-side down reduces moisture loss through the stem scar, the most permeable point on the fruit surface.
storage.room_temp_beginner: About 1 to 2 weeks at room temperature, which is where tomatoes keep their best flavor. Set them stem-side down on the counter, out of direct sun, which helps them hold moisture longer.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Avoid refrigerating ripe tomatoes. Temperatures below 50-55°F cause chilling injury: cell membranes lose their selective permeability, releasing cell-wall-degrading enzymes that produce the mealy texture and muted flavor of cold-stored tomatoes. The damage is irreversible and occurs within hours at refrigerator temperatures. If a ripe tomato must be saved from immediate waste, refrigerate and use within 1-2 days.
storage.fridge_beginner: Try not to refrigerate ripe tomatoes. The cold turns the texture mealy and dulls the flavor, and the damage cannot be undone. If a ripe tomato would otherwise go to waste, you can refrigerate it and use it within a day or two.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Freeze whole for cooking use, do not attempt to eat thawed tomatoes fresh. Freezing ruptures cell walls, making texture mushy when thawed. The practical benefit is that skins slip off easily after thawing, making frozen tomatoes convenient for sauces and cooked dishes. Blanching before freezing is optional but extends storage quality.
storage.freezer_beginner: You can freeze whole tomatoes to cook with later, but do not expect to eat them fresh after thawing: freezing makes the texture mushy. One handy upside is that the skins slip right off once thawed, which is great for sauces and cooked dishes.
storage.notes_beginner: Keep them on the counter, out of direct sun, with the stem scar facing down, which slows moisture loss. Don't stack them in a pile; the weight bruises the ones on the bottom. A single layer in a wide bowl works well.
storage.notes_seasoned: Store at room temperature out of direct sun, stem-side down. Direct sun accelerates softening; stem-side down reduces moisture loss at the stem scar. Do not stack ripe tomatoes in a deep pile, as the weight bruises the bottom layers. A single layer on a countertop or in a wide, shallow bowl works best.

det_indet.detail_beginner: Indeterminate (as explained earlier in this guide) means the plant keeps growing and producing fruit all season long, rather than ripening everything at once and stopping. Almost all cherry tomato varieties work this way, which is part of why they're productive over such a long window. Because they keep growing, they need a sturdy cage or stake to stay upright. A few compact varieties like Tumbling Tom are determinate (they set fruit and stop), which makes them better choices for small containers or hanging baskets.
det_indet.detail_seasoned: Cherry tomatoes are almost always indeterminate: they grow, flower, and fruit all season until frost kills them. No stopping needed, but they need strong staking or caging. Some compact varieties (Tumbling Tom, Patio Choice) are technically determinate.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Tomato seeds need warm soil to sprout, about as warm as a sunny windowsill, or 75°F if you have a soil thermometer. A heating mat under your seed tray is the easiest way to get there. Cover the tray with a clear plastic lid until the first green shoots appear, then take it off.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Tiny white root emerging from the seed, then a pale curved shoot pushing up through the soil. The shoot will straighten and the first two small leaves will unfold at the top.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you seen any sprouts yet?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tiny white root emerging from the seed, then a pale shoot pushing upward through the soil.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep soil temperature in the 70-85°F range. A heat mat makes a real difference for staying in the optimal zone. Cover with a humidity dome until sprouts appear.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you seen any sprouts yet?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: The moment you see the first green sprouts, take off the plastic lid covering your seed tray, as leaving it on causes a fungal problem called damping off that kills seedlings. Move the tray as close to your brightest light as you can get it. If seedlings grow tall and floppy instead of short and stocky, they need more light, not more water; that stretched-out look is called etiolation (reaching for the light), and a weak stem won't fully recover.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Two small flat leaves (the seed leaves) open first, then the first true leaves emerge between them, which will have the distinctive serrated edges and smell of tomato leaves.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How are your seedlings looking?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Two seed leaves open flat, then the first true leaves emerging between them, which will look distinctly tomato-shaped.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Remove the humidity dome the moment the first sprouts appear, as waiting causes damping off. Move seedlings as close to your brightest light source as possible. Tomato seedlings require 14-16 hours of light equivalent to bright natural light to grow compact and stocky; at less than that, they etiolate (stretch toward the light) producing a weak, thin stem that never fully recovers. Leggy seedlings are almost always a light deficiency, not a watering problem.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How are your seedlings looking?

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Before you move seedlings outside, you need to harden them off, meaning giving them short outdoor stints first (start with an hour or two in a sheltered spot), adding more time and sun each day over 7-10 days. Indoor-grown seedlings aren't used to wind, direct sun, or temperature swings; skipping this step shocks the plant and sets it back. When you plant, go deep: bury the stem all the way up to the lowest set of leaves. Tomatoes grow roots from buried stem, so a deeper planting gives you a bigger, more drought-tolerant root system.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The stem is thicker, the plant has 3 or 4 sets of true leaves, and the color is deep green throughout. If you squeeze the stem gently it holds its shape rather than feeling floppy.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are they outside yet, or still hardening off?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong stem, 3-4 sets of true leaves, deep green color. Ready to pot up or transplant.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Begin hardening off 7-10 days before transplant: start with 1-2 hours outdoors in a sheltered spot, extending time and sun exposure each day. Indoor seedlings have thinner cuticles and underdeveloped stomatal regulation, so gradual exposure allows the plant to upregulate protective responses before full outdoor conditions. Plant deep: bury the stem up to the lowest set of leaves. Tomatoes develop adventitious roots from buried stem tissue, so a deeper planting produces a larger, more drought-resistant root system than a shallow one.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are they outside yet, or still hardening off?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: When the first yellow flowers appear, change to a tomato fertilizer (those usually have more potassium, which the plant needs for fruit). Each morning, give the flowering stems a gentle shake or tap. This helps the flowers make fruit, and it really does work, especially indoors or in places without much wind.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Small bright yellow flowers appearing in clusters, each one star-shaped with petals swept back. Each flower is a potential tomato.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Flowers open yet?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small yellow flowers in clusters. Each flower is a potential fruit.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Switch from a balanced fertilizer to a high-potassium, low-nitrogen formulation. Nitrogen drives vegetative growth, which is counterproductive once flowering begins. Potassium governs sugar transport into fruit and is the limiting nutrient for fruit quality and weight at this stage. Gently tap or shake the flowering stems each morning, as tomatoes are self-fertile but require vibration to release pollen efficiently from the anther cone. In still, sheltered environments, this manual step measurably improves fruit set.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Flowers open yet?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pick ripe tomatoes every day or two during peak summer. Ripe fruit left on the vine releases a ripening gas (ethylene) that hurries along the fruit around it, which sounds useful, but in an indeterminate plant that keeps flowering all season, leaving ripe tomatoes hanging too long also pulls the plant's energy away from new flowers and young fruit. Regular picking keeps production moving.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Fruit is fully colored (red, orange, or yellow depending on variety) and gives slightly when you press it gently. Very ripe fruit may start to look a little less shiny than it did.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: First tomatoes picked? Log your harvest.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fully colored fruit that gives slightly to a gentle squeeze. The skin may start to lose its sheen when perfectly ripe.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick regularly, every 1-2 days at peak production. Ripe tomatoes on the vine produce ethylene gas, which accelerates ripening of neighboring fruit and, in indeterminate varieties, can slow the initiation of new flower clusters. Leaving ripe fruit on the vine also creates a physical energy sink: the plant continues investing carbohydrates in already-ripe fruit rather than channeling resources to new flowers and developing fruit.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: First tomatoes picked? Log your harvest.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: When nighttime temperatures stay below 50 degrees regularly, pinch off all the growing tips, the fuzzy little shoots at the ends of each stem. New flowers won't set fruit in that cold anyway (pollen stops working below about 55 degrees at night), and removing the tips redirects the plant's remaining energy into the tomatoes already on the vine. Bring green tomatoes inside before any frost, as they'll keep ripening on a countertop at around 60-65 degrees. Don't refrigerate them: cold below 50 degrees damages the tomato's texture and flavor permanently (this is called chilling injury).
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant is producing fewer new flowers, lower leaves are yellowing, and nights are regularly feeling cold. The plant is winding down.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How was your season? Worth logging what worked.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Slowing production, yellowing lower leaves, nights cooling below 50°F.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: When nights drop below 50°F regularly, pinch out all the growing tips to halt new vegetative growth. Below 55°F, pollen viability declines sharply and new fruit is unlikely to set regardless of how many flowers open. Removing growing tips eliminates the hormone source (auxin from the apical meristem) that pulls resources toward new stem growth, redirecting carbohydrates into the fruit already present on the vine. Bring green tomatoes inside before frost, as they will continue ripening at 60-65°F and store far better than refrigerated tomatoes, which suffer irreversible chilling injury below 50°F.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How was your season? Worth logging what worked.

notifications.title_beginner: Time to start your tomato seeds indoors
notifications.body_beginner: Your last frost date is about {{weeks_until_anchor}} weeks away, now is the right window to start tomato seeds. Fill small trays or cells with seed-starting mix, plant one or two seeds per cell about a quarter inch deep, and put them somewhere warm (70 to 80 degrees is ideal). Cover with a plastic dome or cling wrap until you see sprouts, then remove it right away. This is where your season begins.
notifications.title_seasoned: Time to start your tomatoes indoors
notifications.body_seasoned: Your last frost date is about {{weeks_until_anchor}} weeks away, the perfect window to get tomato seeds into trays. Find somewhere warm (70-80°F), keep the soil consistently moist, and cover with a dome until you see sprouts. This is where your season begins.

notifications.title_beginner: Start introducing your tomatoes to the outdoors
notifications.body_beginner: Your last frost is {{days_until_anchor}} days away, time to start hardening off your seedlings. Put them outside for a couple of hours in a sheltered, partly shaded spot today, then bring them back in. Add more time and more direct sun each day over the next week or two. This gradual transition helps them adapt to wind, sun, and temperature swings before they go out for good.
notifications.body_seasoned: Your last frost is {{days_until_anchor}} days away. Begin putting your plants outside for a few hours each day, starting sheltered and increasing exposure gradually. This week of adjustment makes a real difference to how they settle in after transplanting.

notifications.title_beginner: Frost has passed, your tomatoes are ready to go out
notifications.body_beginner: Now is the time to transplant. Dig a hole deeper than the pot and bury the stem right up to the lowest set of leaves, as roots form all along the buried stem and make for a stronger plant. Water well, and if the weather is still cool, wait for nighttime temps to be consistently above 50 degrees before planting out.
notifications.title_seasoned: Last frost has passed, time to transplant
notifications.body_seasoned: Your tomatoes are ready to go outside for good. Plant them deep: bury the stem right up to the lowest set of leaves. Roots will form all along the buried stem and give you a stronger, more drought-tolerant plant.

notifications.title_beginner: Flowers are coming, switch your fertilizer now
notifications.body_beginner: Small yellow flowers appearing means fruit is on the way. Switch to a tomato fertilizer or a high-potassium fertilizer now (look for a bag with the third number largest, like 5-10-10). Gently shaking the flower stems in the morning helps pollen move between flowers. Each flower is a potential tomato.
notifications.title_seasoned: Your tomatoes should be flowering soon
notifications.body_seasoned: Small yellow flowers appearing means fruit is on the way. Switch to a high-potassium feed now, and give the flowering stems a gentle shake in the morning to help pollination. Each flower is a potential tomato.

notifications.title_beginner: Your first tomatoes should be nearly ready
notifications.body_beginner: Based on when you planted, ripe or almost-ripe fruit should be appearing now. Pick when the tomato is fully colored and gives slightly when you press it gently. The more you pick, the more the plant produces, so check the plant every day or two once fruit starts coming in.
notifications.title_seasoned: First tomatoes should be nearly ready
notifications.body_seasoned: Based on when you planted, you should be seeing ripe or nearly-ripe fruit about now. Pick when fully colored and slightly soft to the touch. The more you pick, the more the plant produces, so stay on top of it.

notifications.title_beginner: Frost coming in {{weeks_until_anchor}} weeks, time to finish strong
notifications.body_beginner: Your growing season is nearly over. Pinch out the growing tips at the top of each stem now so the plant puts its remaining energy into ripening the fruit already there rather than growing new stems. Harvest everything you can, and bring in any green tomatoes, as they will ripen on a windowsill indoors over the next few weeks.
notifications.title_seasoned: First frost in {{weeks_until_anchor}} weeks, finish strong
notifications.body_seasoned: Your growing season is almost done. Pinch out the growing tips now so the plant puts all its remaining energy into the fruit already on the vine. Harvest anything you can and bring green tomatoes inside to ripen on a windowsill.

notifications.title_beginner: How are your tomatoes doing?
notifications.body_beginner: You haven't logged anything in a couple of weeks. How does the plant look? Any fruit coming in, any spots on the leaves, or anything that looks off? Catching problems early makes a big difference, and a quick look around the plant takes two minutes.
notifications.body_seasoned: You have not logged anything in a couple of weeks. How is the plant looking? Any flowers, fruit, or pests worth noting? Regular check-ins help you catch problems early.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost tonight, cover your tomatoes
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Freezing temperatures are forecast tonight. Tomatoes are frost-tender and one hard freeze can kill the plant. Cover them with an old bedsheet, a bucket, or frost cloth before dark, and uncover in the morning once temperatures are back above freezing. Container plants can be moved inside.
weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning, protect your tomatoes tonight
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Temperatures are dropping close to freezing tonight. Cover plants with fleece or old bedsheets, or bring containers inside. Tomatoes are frost-tender and one cold night can end your season early.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Very hot days ahead, help your tomatoes through
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Several very hot days are forecast. Above about 95 degrees, tomato flowers tend to drop without setting fruit, not a disease, just heat stress. Water deeply in the early morning so the soil stays moist through the day, and add a layer of mulch around the base to hold that moisture. If you have shade cloth, draping it over the plant in the hottest part of the afternoon can help.
weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat stress warning for your tomatoes
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Several very hot days ahead. Tomato flowers can drop when temperatures stay above 95°F. Water deeply in the early morning, add mulch around the base to retain moisture, and consider shade cloth during the hottest part of the day.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: It's been dry, water your tomatoes deeply
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Dry conditions have been building. Uneven watering right now can cause blossom end rot (dark patches on the fruit bottom) and cracked fruit. Water deeply at the base of the plant, aiming for 1 to 2 inches this week. A thick layer of mulch around the stem helps hold whatever moisture the soil has between watering sessions.
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: It has been dry. Inconsistent watering at this stage causes blossom end rot and cracked fruit. Water deeply at the base, aiming for 1-2 inches this week. Mulching around the stem helps hold moisture.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: High humidity, check your tomato leaves
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Humid weather creates ideal conditions for fungal diseases like early and late blight. Take a few minutes to check the lower leaves for brown spots, yellow patches, or anything unusual. If you spot affected leaves, remove them right away and don't put them in your compost. Keeping the plant staked and open for airflow is your best prevention.
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Humid conditions are ideal for early and late blight. Check lower leaves for dark spots with yellow halos. Remove any affected leaves immediately and do not compost them. Good airflow around the plant is your best defense.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Heavy rain coming, harvest ripe tomatoes now
weather_triggers.body_beginner: A lot of rain in a short period can cause ripe tomatoes to split. Pick anything that looks close to ready before the rain arrives. After the rain, check the lower leaves, as soil splash from heavy rain can spread disease spores up onto the leaves.
weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heavy rain, harvest ripe tomatoes now
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A lot of rain in a short time can split ripe fruit. Pick anything that is nearly ready before it cracks, and check for soil splash on lower leaves which can spread disease.

germination.text_beginner: Bottom heat is the single biggest factor in germination speed. If you have a heat mat, use it; if not, the top of a refrigerator or any spot that stays around 75 degrees works well. Most cherry tomato seeds sprout in 5 to 7 days with steady warmth.
germination.text_seasoned: Bottom heat is the single biggest factor in germination speed. A heat mat, the top of your refrigerator, or anywhere consistently warm works well. Most tomato seeds germinate in 5-7 days at 75°F.

germination.text_beginner: Cover your seed tray with a plastic dome or cling wrap until the first sprout appears, then remove it immediately. The dome traps humidity to keep the seed surface moist during germination, but once the shoot emerges, that same warm, still air is the ideal environment for damping off, a fungal problem that collapses the stem at the soil line and kills the seedling overnight with no recovery. Remove the dome at first sprout and give the seedlings fresh air; slightly drier conditions at the soil surface prevent it.
germination.text_seasoned: Cover your tray with a humidity dome or cling film until the first sprout appears, then remove it immediately. The dome holds humidity to prevent the seed surface from drying out during germination, but once the shoot emerges the same warm, still, humid air becomes the ideal environment for Pythium and Rhizoctonia, the soilborne fungi that cause damping off. Damping off collapses the stem at soil level; there is no recovery. Fresh air and slightly drier conditions at the soil surface after emergence are the primary prevention.

seedling.text_beginner: If your seedlings are tall and thin and look weak, they need more light, not less water. Move them right next to a bright window (but pull them back a few inches at night if the window gets cold), or set up a grow light to shine on them for 14-16 hours each day. Pale color is a sign of the same problem.
seedling.text_seasoned: Leggy, stretched seedlings almost always mean not enough light, not overwatering. Get them as close to a bright window as possible, or use a grow light 14-16 hours a day.

seedling.text_beginner: Once you have two sets of true leaves, move the seedling into its own small pot or 3-inch cell. Tomatoes root all along their stems, so plant it a little deeper than it was sitting, as the buried stem becomes more roots.
seedling.text_seasoned: Once you have two sets of true leaves, pot up into individual cells or small 3-inch pots. Tomatoes root all along their stems, so you can bury them deeper than they were, which builds a stronger plant.

established.text_beginner: Hardening off takes 7 to 10 days and is worth every day of it. The seedlings have been raised in still indoor air with no wind or direct sun, and their leaves aren't built for outdoor conditions yet. Start with 1 to 2 hours outside in a sheltered, partly shaded spot, then add more time and more sun each day. Plants that are hardened off gradually settle in within a week of transplanting; plants that skip it can take 3 weeks to recover.
established.text_seasoned: Harden off over 7-10 days, a gradual introduction to outdoor conditions rather than an abrupt move. Indoors, seedlings have thin cuticles, less concentrated chlorophyll, and stomata that have never experienced wind. Sudden outdoor exposure causes sunscald, wilting, and cold stress even on mild days. Start with 1-2 hours in a sheltered, partly shaded spot, adding time and sun exposure each day. Plants that skip hardening off sulk for 2-3 weeks after transplanting while they adapt.

established.text_beginner: Plant your tomatoes deeper than the pot they came in. Dig a hole deep enough to bury the stem right up to the lowest set of leaves, as every bit of buried stem grows roots, and more roots means a stronger, more drought-tolerant plant from day one.
established.text_seasoned: Plant your tomatoes deeper than they sit in the pot. Bury the stem right up to the lowest set of leaves. Every bit of buried stem becomes roots.

flowering.text_beginner: Give the flowering stems a gentle shake or tap in the morning to help with pollination. Tomato flowers release pollen when they vibrate, and bees do this naturally, but in sheltered gardens or when bee activity is low, giving the stems a quick shake does the same job. Without it, some flowers drop before setting fruit.
flowering.text_seasoned: A gentle shake or tap of the flowering stem in the morning helps pollen transfer. Tomato flowers are self-fertile, but pollen is released most efficiently by vibration: bumblebees accomplish this naturally through buzz pollination, where wing-beat frequency resonates the anthers and dislodges pollen. In sheltered gardens, polytunnels, or indoor growing environments without significant wind or bee activity, the plant depends on incidental vibration for pollination. Shaking the stem in the morning (when pollen is freshly released) is the practical substitute. Under-pollinated flowers drop without setting fruit.

flowering.text_beginner: Once flowers open, stop any high-nitrogen fertilizer and switch to a tomato fertilizer or one with a high third number (potassium). Nitrogen is what makes plants grow leaves, exactly right early on but exactly wrong once flowering starts. Potassium is what the plant needs to build good fruit.
flowering.text_seasoned: Stop high-nitrogen feeding when flowers appear and switch to a high-potassium, low-nitrogen feed. Nitrogen drives vegetative growth by stimulating cell division and chlorophyll synthesis, exactly what you want early in the season and exactly what you don't want once flowering starts; potassium plays a different role: it regulates stomatal opening, drives sugar transport from leaves into developing fruit, and is critical for cell wall formation in the fruit itself. A tomato-specific or high-K fertilizer (look for an NPK ratio with a high last number, such as 5-10-10 or 4-12-8) used from first flowering onward translates directly into heavier, better-flavored fruit.

harvest.text_beginner: Pick regularly, every day or two once fruit is coming in. Leaving ripe tomatoes on the vine slows the plant's production of new fruit, especially with indeterminate varieties like most cherry tomatoes.
harvest.text_seasoned: Pick regularly, as ripe fruit left on the vine slows new fruit production, especially in indeterminate varieties.

harvest.text_beginner: Try a few tomatoes at different stages to find what your palate likes. Some varieties are sweetest just at peak color; others improve with a few more days. Your own taste is the best harvest guide you have.
harvest.text_seasoned: Taste as you go. Different varieties peak at different moments: some are best just before fully ripe, others need a few more days. Your palate is the best harvest indicator you have.

end_of_season.text_beginner: When nights drop regularly below 50 degrees, pinch out the growing tips, the very top of each stem. Below 55 degrees, tomatoes stop setting new fruit reliably. By removing the growing tips, you redirect the plant's energy into ripening the fruit already on the vine rather than trying to grow new stems that won't produce before frost.
end_of_season.text_seasoned: When nights drop regularly below 50°F, pinch out all the growing tips. Below 55°F, pollen viability drops sharply and fruit set becomes unlikely even if flowers are still opening. At 50°F and below, the plant is physiologically in decline for new fruit production. Pinching the growing tips, the terminal bud at the top of each stem, removes the hormone sink that draws resources toward new vegetative growth, redirecting carbohydrates toward the fruit already on the vine. A plant with 10-15 near-ripe tomatoes will finish them faster once it has stopped trying to grow new stems.

end_of_season.text_beginner: Green tomatoes brought in before frost will ripen indoors. Lay them in a single layer somewhere cool (60 to 65 degrees) and dark, not the refrigerator. Refrigerator temperatures cause chilling injury, which produces the mealy, flavorless texture that makes people think they dislike tomatoes. Room temperature speeds ripening but hurts flavor; 60 to 65 degrees is the right balance.
end_of_season.text_seasoned: Green tomatoes left on the plant when frost threatens can be brought inside to ripen. Lay them in a single layer somewhere cool (60-65°F) and dark, not the refrigerator. Refrigerator temperatures (below 50°F) cause chilling injury: cell membranes in the fruit lose their selective permeability, releasing enzymes that break down cell walls, producing the mealy texture and muted flavor characteristic of cold-stored tomatoes. The damage is irreversible once it occurs. Ripening indoors at 60-65°F is slower than at room temperature but preserves flavor better than hurrying at 70°F+.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 4-8 lbs over the season per plant, with cherry-type hybrids commonly producing at the upper end of that range under good conditions. Indeterminate varieties continue producing until frost; determinate cherry types produce a concentrated flush and then taper off.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: About 4 to 8 pounds of fruit per plant over the season, and cherry types often land at the higher end when conditions are good. Vining (indeterminate) plants keep producing until frost; bushier (determinate) plants give one big flush and then taper off.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: At peak a healthy indeterminate plant yields a generous bowlful every 2-3 days. Production is not linear: it accelerates from first harvest, peaks in the hottest weeks of summer, and then slows in late season as temperatures drop and days shorten.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: At its peak, a healthy vining plant gives you a generous bowlful every 2 to 3 days. Production is not steady: it builds up after the first few tomatoes, peaks in the hottest weeks of summer, then slows down as the season cools and the days get shorter.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Your first year, expect to land somewhere in the lower part of the range while you learn what your specific spot needs. The four things that make the biggest difference are sun (at least 6 hours of direct sun daily), consistent watering, good soil, and catching pest or disease problems early. If you're picking enough tomatoes to fill a salad bowl every week or two, that is a real first-season success.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: First-season plants often yield at the low end of the range as growers learn site-specific conditions. Soil organic matter, sun hours, consistent watering, and timely disease response each contribute materially to where within the 4-8 lb range a plant lands. Getting enough tomatoes to fill a salad bowl regularly is a genuine first-season success.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: You'll see the leaves turn black or dark brown and go limp, sometimes overnight after a cold night. Tomatoes have no cold tolerance at all. Even without a hard freeze, temperatures below 50 degrees cause what's called chilling injury: the plant's cells start to break down, and young transplants are especially vulnerable because they haven't built up a protective waxy coating yet. It's tempting to think the plant just needs time to recover, but if it was hit by frost, it usually won't come back. For next time: wait until both your nighttime lows and your soil temperature are reliably above 60 degrees before transplanting.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Wait until nighttime temperatures are reliably above 50 degrees AND your soil is above 60 degrees before transplanting, checking soil temperature 2 to 3 inches deep with an inexpensive probe thermometer. In Zones 3 to 5 this often means waiting until late May or early June no matter what the calendar says.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Tomatoes are warm-season crops with tropical origin and have no cold tolerance mechanism, unlike brassicas or root vegetables, they cannot harden or acclimate to cold. Chilling injury begins below 50°F and cell damage accelerates near freezing; a single frost event at the transplant stage usually kills the plant outright because young transplants have not yet developed the protective waxy cuticle layer that provides some buffer in established plants. Soil temperature is as important as air temperature: roots in cold soil (below 60°F) cannot take up water or nutrients efficiently even when air temperatures are acceptable, which causes transplant shock that looks like cold damage but persists for weeks after the weather improves.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait until both nighttime air temperatures are reliably above 50°F and soil temperature is above 60°F before transplanting. Check soil temperature with a probe thermometer 2-3 inches deep in the actual planting bed, as a south-facing raised bed can be 10°F warmer than a shaded in-ground bed on the same day. In zones 3-5, this means waiting until late May or even early June, regardless of calendar date.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Tomato plants can run into a few common problems. Blight is a leaf disease that shows up first on the bottom leaves and spreads fastest in wet, humid weather. Blossom end rot is the black or brown sunken spot on the bottom of the tomato, it looks like a nutrient problem, but it's almost always caused by uneven watering (dry one day, soaked the next). Adding calcium won't fix it. Steady moisture will.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Water at the base of the plant (not from overhead) and stake the plant for good airflow, as leaves that dry quickly after rain are far harder for blight to infect. Move your tomatoes to a different bed each year; blight spores can persist in the soil and on old plant material. For blossom end rot: mulch heavily and water deeply and consistently rather than in small, frequent amounts.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Two of the most common problems, blight and blossom end rot, are frequently misdiagnosed and mistreated. Blight (early or late) is a fungal or oomycete disease that enters through wet leaf surfaces; spores splash up from soil and spread rapidly in warm, humid conditions, progressing from lower leaves upward. Removing affected leaves immediately slows but does not stop spread once established. Blossom end rot presents as a sunken, dark patch on the blossom end of developing fruit. Despite appearances, it is not a fungal disease and adding calcium to the soil rarely fixes it. The actual mechanism is calcium transport failure: calcium moves into developing fruit through the water stream in the xylem, and when watering is inconsistent, especially dry periods followed by heavy irrigation, the transpiration-driven flow to the blossom end is interrupted, and those cells die. Steady moisture at the root zone is the only reliable fix.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water at the base, never overhead, to eliminate the splash route that delivers blight spores to leaves. Stake and prune for airflow, as leaves that dry quickly after rain or dew are far less vulnerable. Rotate tomatoes to a different bed each year; blight spores persist in soil and on plant debris, and a fresh location breaks the inoculum cycle. For blossom end rot: mulch heavily to buffer moisture swings, and water deeply and consistently rather than shallowly and frequently.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Yellow lower leaves and wilting, even when the soil is wet, are the signs you've overwatered. Soggy soil pushes out the air the roots need to breathe; once roots suffocate, the plant can't take up water even though there's plenty of it, which is why it wilts. People often respond by watering more, which makes things worse. Cracked fruit is a related but separate problem: it happens when you water heavily after a dry stretch, the tomato swells fast and the skin splits. The fix is consistency: aim for steady moisture rather than long dry spells followed by big waterings.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Water deeply and less often rather than a little every day. Deep watering encourages roots to grow down where the soil stays more stable; roots near the surface are the first to suffocate or dry out. A 2 to 3 inch layer of mulch around the base dramatically reduces moisture swings between waterings.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Waterlogged soil drives out the oxygen roots need for cellular respiration, so roots in anaerobic conditions die back, and without functioning roots the plant cannot take up water or nutrients even as the soil stays wet. Yellowing lower leaves are the first visible sign, followed by generalized wilting that paradoxically looks like drought. Fruit cracking is a related but distinct problem: it happens when a sudden surge of water (heavy rain after a dry period, or a large irrigation after letting the plant get too dry) causes rapid fruit cell expansion in a skin that has already stopped stretching. The skin splits at the shoulders or develops concentric cracks. Both problems are rooted in inconsistency rather than sheer total volume, as a plant that receives consistent 1-2 inches per week rarely cracks or shows root oxygen stress.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water deeply and less frequently rather than a small amount every day. Deep watering (wetting the soil to 8-10 inches) encourages roots to grow down where soil moisture is more stable; shallow watering concentrates roots at the surface where they are most vulnerable to both drought and saturation. Mulching 2-3 inches around the base dramatically reduces moisture swings between waterings, which is the single most effective intervention against both fruit cracking and blossom end rot.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Flowers dropping before they form fruit and dark sunken patches on the bottom of tomatoes are the two big signs of insufficient or uneven watering. When water gets cut off during flowering, the plant sheds its flowers to conserve resources, physically cutting them loose at the stem. The dark patch on the fruit's base is called blossom end rot; it looks like a nutrient problem but it's almost always caused by uneven soil moisture, not a lack of calcium in your soil. People often add calcium supplements, but that won't fix it; steady, consistent watering will. Note that heat above 90 degrees causes the same flower-drop, so both can happen at the same time.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Aim for 1 to 2 inches of water per week, delivered consistently. Mulch around the base with straw or shredded leaves to slow the soil from drying out. In hot climates (Zones 8 to 11), a drip line on a timer is the most reliable way to keep moisture steady without thinking about it every day.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Water stress during flowering triggers an abscission response: the plant activates an enzyme-driven separation layer at the base of each flower stem, dropping the flower before fruit can form. The same response is triggered by extreme heat (above 90°F daytime, below 55°F nighttime), which means during a heat wave, blossom drop can occur even if the soil seems adequately moist. During fruit development, inconsistent soil moisture is the primary cause of blossom end rot: calcium is transported to developing fruit through the transpiration stream, and interrupted water flow to the blossom end kills those cells. The external result is a sunken, darkened patch on the fruit's base.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Aim for 1-2 inches of water per week delivered consistently. Mulch heavily around the base to buffer the soil against rapid drying, as a 2-3 inch layer of straw or shredded leaves can halve moisture loss on a hot day. In zones 8-11, where summer heat makes consistent moisture especially difficult, a drip system on a timer is the most reliable tool. Water at the base of the plant, never the leaves.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: If your plant grows tall and leafy but produces very little fruit, or pale, flavorless tomatoes, sun is probably the problem. Tomatoes need at least 6 hours of direct sun per day; below that, the plant puts its energy into growing stems and leaves instead of fruit. What fruit does form tends to be bland because sugar development depends on sunlight. A secondary sign: shaded plants tend to stay wet longer and get more disease, because leaves don't dry out well in low light. If your spot gets 4-5 hours, you'll get some fruit, but manage expectations: fewer tomatoes, smaller, and less sweet than a full-sun plant.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Tomatoes need at least 6 hours of direct sun per day, and this is not negotiable. If your current spot is borderline, walk your garden at different times of day and look for a spot a few feet over that gets more morning sun before something shades it. Compact cherry tomato varieties like dwarf or patio types tolerate slightly less sun than full-size plants.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Tomatoes are among the most light-demanding vegetables: photosynthesis is the energy source for both vegetative growth and fruit sugar development, and fruit quality is directly proportional to the plant's photosynthetic output. Below 6 hours of direct sun, the plant redirects what energy it has toward survival, stem elongation and leaf area, rather than reproduction. Fruit set drops sharply, and what fruit does form is typically thin-skinned, pale, and bland. A secondary effect is increased disease: shaded plants stay wetter longer after rain or irrigation, and poor airflow through dense, etiolated growth creates the humid microclimate that blight and leaf mold need to establish.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Tomatoes are not negotiable on sun requirements. Below 6 hours of direct sun, expect significantly reduced yields and higher disease pressure regardless of everything else done correctly. If the current spot is marginal (6-7 hours), it is worth mapping sun across the garden before committing the bed again, as a spot that gets shade from a fence or tree in the afternoon may have 2-3 more hours of morning sun available just a few feet away. Dwarf or patio-type cherry tomatoes tolerate slightly less sun than full-size plants.
