rotation.note_beginner: If you have no choice but to replant where a stone fruit was, dig out and replace a big area of soil, pick a tougher rootstock like Guardian if nematodes are a worry, and expect the tree to start slower. The simplest fix is to plant in a new spot instead.

growth_stages.name: Planting (bare-root, dormant)
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Late winter to early spring, while the tree is dormant and leafless, as soon as the soil can be worked.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Late winter or early spring, while the young tree is still bare and leafless and the ground can be dug.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A dormant bare-root whip or branched tree with firm, plump buds and healthy, unbroken roots. The graft union (the swollen joint where the variety meets the rootstock) should sit a couple of inches above the final soil line.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A leafless young tree with firm buds and healthy roots. Find the graft union, the swollen joint low on the trunk where your peach variety was joined to its rootstock (the root system it grows on). Keep that joint a couple of inches above the soil when you plant.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Dig a hole as wide as the roots spread and no deeper than they sat in the nursery, spread the roots, and set the tree at the same depth with the graft union above grade. Backfill with native soil, water in well to settle it, and do not bury the trunk.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Dig a hole wide enough for the roots to spread and only as deep as they were growing before. Set the tree at that same depth, keeping the graft joint above the soil. Fill in with the soil you dug out, water well to settle it, and never pile soil up the trunk.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record the planting date and the cultivar and rootstock you set.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note the day you planted, and which peach variety and rootstock it is.

growth_stages.name: Year-one establishment
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: The first full growing season after planting.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: The first whole growing season after you plant the tree.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Steady new shoot growth and a strengthening root system. Any blossoms that form in the first year should be removed so the tree spends its energy on roots and framework rather than fruit.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Healthy new shoots and a tree settling in. If it tries to flower in this first year, pick the flowers off so the tree puts its energy into roots and branches instead of fruit.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply and regularly through the first season so the roots establish (this is the tree's most water-sensitive period), keep a weed-free, mulched circle around the trunk without piling mulch against the bark, and remove first-year flowers. Begin training the framework with light formative pruning.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Water deeply and often this first season, since a new tree needs steady water to get its roots going. Keep a mulched, weed-free circle around the trunk, but keep the mulch off the bark. Remove any flowers this year, and begin shaping the branches with light pruning.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Log first-season watering and the date you removed first-year blossoms.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note your watering and the day you removed the first-year flowers.

growth_stages.name: Scaffold formation (years one to three)
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: The first three years, the framework-building phase before reliable bearing.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: The first three years, while you are building the tree's main branches and before it fruits much.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Peaches are trained to an open-center (vase) shape: three to five well-spaced main scaffold limbs radiating from a short trunk, with an open middle that lets light and air reach all the fruit. Watch for crossing, inward, or overly upright shoots to remove.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Peaches are usually trained to an open-center or vase shape: three to five evenly spaced main branches (called scaffolds) coming off a short trunk, with an open middle. This lets light and air reach all the fruit. Look for branches that cross, head inward, or shoot straight up to remove.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Each late dormant season, select and keep the best-placed scaffolds and remove competing, crossing, and inward growth to maintain the open center. Peach fruits on one-year-old wood, so this annual renewal pruning also keeps fresh fruiting wood coming.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Each year in late winter, keep the best-placed main branches and cut away ones that cross, crowd, or grow inward, keeping the center open. Peaches fruit on wood that grew the year before, so this yearly pruning also keeps new fruiting wood coming.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record each dormant-season pruning and the scaffolds retained.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you prune each winter and which main branches you kept.

growth_stages.name: Winter dormancy
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Roughly December through February, the leafless months when the tree banks chill.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: About December through February, the leafless winter months.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A leafless tree at rest. During these cold months the tree accumulates chill hours (time between 32 and 45°F) that it needs to break dormancy and bloom evenly in spring. There is little to see, but the cold is doing essential work.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A bare, resting tree. Through these cold months the tree is collecting chill hours, the cold time it needs (hours between 32 and 45°F) before it will bloom properly in spring. There is not much to see, but the cold matters.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Little is required beyond the dormant-season tasks: this is the window for the dormant fungicide spray where leaf curl is a concern, and for clearing any mummified fruit and fallen debris that harbor disease. Established trees need minimal water now.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Not much to do beyond the winter tasks: this is when to apply the dormant copper spray if leaf curl is a problem in your area, and to clear away any dried mummy fruit and fallen debris that carry disease. An established tree needs very little water now.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Note the dormant spray date and any winter sanitation.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you did the dormant spray and any winter cleanup.

growth_stages.name: Dormant pruning
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Late dormancy, roughly February into March, just before growth resumes.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Late winter, around February into March, just before the tree wakes up.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare branches that show the tree's structure clearly. This is the moment to read the open-center framework and the balance of one-year-old fruiting wood before the buds swell.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Bare branches, so you can see the whole shape of the tree. This is the easiest time to judge the framework and the fresh fruiting wood before the buds swell.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Prune annually in late dormancy: maintain the open center, remove dead, diseased, crossing, and downward wood, and head back to renew a supply of vigorous one-year shoots, since peach bears on last year's growth. Peaches are pruned harder than most fruit trees. Make clean cuts to avoid the wounds that invite borers and canker.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Prune every year in late winter: keep the center open, cut out dead, diseased, crossing, and downward branches, and shorten growth to keep new vigorous shoots coming, since peaches fruit on last year's wood. Peaches get pruned harder than most fruit trees. Make clean cuts, because ragged wounds invite borers and canker.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record the dormant pruning date and how heavily you cut.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note the day you pruned and how much you took off.

growth_stages.name: Bloom
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Early spring, the exact timing shifting by region from February on the Gulf to April in the North.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Early spring. The exact week depends on where you live, earlier in warm areas, later in cold ones.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Pink blossoms opening across the tree. Most peaches are self-fertile, so a single tree sets fruit on its own. This is also the most frost-vulnerable moment of the year: open blossoms and tiny fruit are killed by a hard late frost.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Pink flowers opening all over the tree. Most peaches are self-fertile, meaning one tree can set fruit by itself. This is also the riskiest time for frost: an open flower or a tiny new peach can be killed by a hard late frost.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Watch the frost forecast closely; if a hard frost threatens open bloom, a backyard tree can sometimes be protected with a cover overnight. In a wet bloom, this is the window for a brown-rot blossom spray. Otherwise let the tree set its own crop.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep an eye on the frost forecast. If a hard frost is coming while the tree is in bloom, you can sometimes protect a small tree by covering it overnight. If bloom is wet, this is the time for a brown-rot spray. Otherwise just let the tree set its fruit.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record the bloom date and any frost-protection or bloom spray.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when bloom started and anything you did for frost or spray.

growth_stages.name: Fruit set and thinning
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Spring, after petal fall, once young fruit has formed and sized to about marble stage.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Spring, after the petals drop, once small green peaches have formed and are about marble-sized.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Heavy clusters of small green fruit. Peaches characteristically overset, and an unthinned tree produces many small, poor-quality peaches and risks limb breakage from the weight.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Lots of small green peaches, often crowded together. Peaches usually set far more fruit than the tree can size well, so without thinning you get many small, poor peaches and branches can break under the load.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin the young fruit to roughly one peach every 6 to 8 inches along the branch, removing the rest while they are small. This is the single biggest lever on fruit size and quality, and it protects the limbs. Thinning also removes some insect-damaged fruit early.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Thin the little fruits so that about one peach is left every 6 to 8 inches along each branch, picking off the extras while they are small. This one step does more for fruit size and quality than anything else, and it keeps branches from breaking. It also lets you remove damaged fruit early.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record the thinning date and the spacing you thinned to.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you thinned and how far apart you left the peaches.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Summer, the month varying widely by variety and region; first reliable crop around year three.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Summer. The exact time depends on the variety and your area. Most trees give their first real crop around year three.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Ripe peaches lose their green undertone, take on full variety color, give slightly to gentle pressure, and pull free with a slight twist. Aroma is a strong cue. A tree ripens over one to two weeks, not all at once, so it is picked in several passes.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A ripe peach loses its green tinge, shows full color, gives a little when gently squeezed, and comes off with a slight twist. A ripe smell is a good sign. The tree ripens over one to two weeks rather than all at once, so you pick it a few times.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick in several passes as fruit ripens, handling gently to avoid bruises that invite brown rot. Eat or use tree-ripe fruit quickly, or chill promptly. Clear any rotted or dropped fruit as you go so it does not seed disease.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pick over several days as the peaches ripen, handling them gently so they do not bruise (bruises invite brown rot). Eat or use ripe fruit quickly, or put it in the fridge. Pick up any rotted or dropped fruit so it does not spread disease.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record harvest dates and a rough yield.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you picked and roughly how much you got.

notifications.title_beginner: Time to plant your peach tree
notifications.body_seasoned: Set a dormant bare-root tree now, while it is still leafless and the ground is workable. Keep the graft union (the swollen knuckle where the top variety joins the root) two to three inches above the final soil line, pick a full-sun, well-drained spot away from frost pockets, and head the tree back at planting to start the open-center scaffold.
notifications.body_beginner: Now is the time to plant a bare-root peach, while it is still dormant (leafless and resting) and the soil can be dug. Keep the graft union, the swollen bump low on the trunk, about two to three inches above the soil, and choose a sunny spot with good drainage that does not sit in a low, frosty dip. Cut the young tree back at planting to start its shape.

notifications.title_beginner: Time to prune your peach
notifications.body_seasoned: Prune now, in late dormancy just before buds swell. Peaches bear on one-year-old wood and are pruned harder than most fruit trees, so this annual renewal cut is essential, not optional, for a steady crop. Keep the center open, make clean cuts, and remove any cankered wood that invites borers.
notifications.body_beginner: Prune now, in late winter just before the buds start to swell. Peaches make their fruit on wood that grew last year, so cutting back hard every year, more than other fruit trees, is what keeps the crop coming. Open up the middle of the tree, make clean cuts, and take out any dead or oozing wood.

notifications.title_seasoned: Bloom is open, watch for late frost
notifications.title_beginner: Flowers are open, watch the frost
notifications.body_seasoned: Your tree is flowering, which is the year's highest-risk stretch for the crop: a hard freeze on open blossoms or just-set fruit can take all of it. Watch the overnight lows through bloom, and cover a small tree if a hard late frost is forecast. Most peaches are self-fertile and set alone, so no second tree is needed unless you grow a variety like J.H. Hale.
notifications.body_beginner: Open flowers are the moment a peach crop is most at risk from frost: one hard freeze on the blossoms or tiny new fruit can wipe out the year's peaches. Watch the overnight forecast while the tree is in bloom, and drape a cover over a small tree if a hard frost is coming. Most peaches make fruit on their own, so you do not need a second tree unless you planted a variety like J.H. Hale.

notifications.title_beginner: Time to thin the peaches
notifications.body_seasoned: Once the tree has finished its natural June drop, thin the remaining fruit to one peach every six to eight inches. Thinning is the single biggest lever on final fruit size and the main protection against limbs breaking under an overset crop. Take off any insect-scarred fruit as you go.
notifications.body_beginner: After the tree drops some small fruit on its own in early summer, thin what is left to one peach every six to eight inches (about a hand's width apart). Removing extra fruit is the biggest thing you can do to grow large peaches, and it keeps branches from snapping under too heavy a load. Pull off any fruit with insect marks while you are at it.

notifications.title_beginner: Water your new tree deeply
notifications.body_seasoned: Through its first two seasons a peach is at its most water-sensitive while roots establish. Water deeply and regularly at the root zone, by drip or soaker, and avoid wetting the canopy, which feeds brown rot. Keep a weed-free, mulched circle around the trunk so the tree is not competing for moisture.
notifications.body_beginner: For its first couple of years, a young peach needs steady water while its roots get going. Give it a deep soak at the ground every week or so (a drip line or soaker hose is ideal) rather than spraying the leaves, since wet leaves invite disease. Keep a mulched, weed-free ring around the trunk so weeds are not stealing the water.

notifications.title_beginner: Peaches are sizing up, harvest soon
notifications.body_seasoned: The last two to four weeks before harvest are the make-or-break window: most of the fruit's final size is added now, and water stress causes irreversible loss that later watering cannot recover. Keep moisture steady. A peach is ready when the ground color shifts from green to warm yellow, the flesh gives slightly near the stem, and the fruit pulls free with a gentle twist. A tree ripens over one to two weeks, so pick in several passes.
notifications.body_beginner: Peaches gain most of their size in the final few weeks, so keep the watering steady right up to harvest; letting the tree dry out now leaves you with small fruit for good. A peach is ripe when its background color turns from green to warm yellow, it gives a little near the stem, and it pulls off with a gentle twist. The tree ripens over a week or two, so pick a few at a time instead of all at once.

notifications.title_beginner: Clean up for winter
notifications.body_seasoned: As the tree drops its leaves, clear every mummified fruit from the branches and the ground and rake up fallen debris. These are the overwintering source of brown rot for next spring, so this cleanup is your cheapest disease control. Late summer through fall is also the window to check the trunk base for fresh gum and frass that signal borers.
notifications.body_beginner: As the leaves fall, pick off any shriveled, dried-up fruit still hanging on the tree, gather what dropped, and rake up the litter underneath. That old fruit is where the brown rot disease waits out the winter, so clearing it is the easiest way to prevent it. It is also a good time to check the bottom of the trunk for fresh sap or sawdust, which can mean borers.

notifications.title_seasoned: Anything to log on the peach?
notifications.title_beginner: How is your peach tree doing?
notifications.body_seasoned: It has been a while since your last note. A quick check pays off on a tree: scan for fresh gum or frass at the trunk base, confirm any mummified fruit is gone, and note where bloom and harvest landed this year so you can compare next season. Logging the dates now makes your tree's pattern clearer over time.
notifications.body_beginner: It has been a while since you logged anything. A quick look at the tree is worth it: check the base of the trunk for sap or sawdust, make sure no old dried fruit is left hanging, and jot down when the tree bloomed and when you picked. Writing the dates down now helps you see the tree's rhythm year to year.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost warning while flowering
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A hard freeze on open bloom or newly set fruit is the single most common way a peach crop is lost. If a frost is forecast tonight, cover a small tree before evening to trap ground warmth, and water the soil beforehand, since moist ground holds and releases more heat overnight. Large trees are hard to protect, which is why a frost-aware site and a later-blooming variety matter most.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: A hard frost on open flowers or tiny new fruit is the most common reason a peach crop fails. If frost is forecast tonight, cover a small tree before dark to hold in the ground's warmth, and water the soil first, since damp ground stays warmer overnight. Big trees are hard to cover, so the best protection is planting somewhere less frost-prone and choosing a variety that blooms later.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Muggy weather, watch for rot
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Warm, humid conditions drive brown rot, the fungus that browns blossoms at bloom and can rot a ripening peach within a day or two. There is no spraying it away mid-spell: keep the canopy open and dry, water only at the root zone, remove any rotting fruit promptly, and harvest ripe fruit without delay so it is off the tree before the rot reaches it.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Warm, muggy weather is what brown rot loves, the disease that turns blossoms brown and can rot a ripe peach in a day or two. You cannot spray it away once it is muggy, so keep the tree open and the leaves dry, water only at the ground, pick off any rotting fruit right away, and harvest ripe peaches promptly so they are off the tree before the rot finds them.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Heavy rain, watch ripe fruit
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A wet canopy feeds brown rot and leaf disease, and rain on nearly ripe fruit can crack and rot it on the tree. After a soaking rain, check ripening peaches and pick any that are ready rather than leaving them to split. An open canopy that dries fast after rain is your best standing defense.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Wet leaves and fruit invite disease, and rain on almost-ripe peaches can split and rot them right on the branch. After a heavy rain, look over the ripening fruit and pick anything that is ready instead of leaving it to crack. Keeping the tree open so it dries quickly after rain is the best ongoing protection.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Dry stretch, keep up deep watering
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Dry spell, do not let the tree run dry
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: During a dry stretch, deep, regular watering matters most in two windows: a first-year tree establishing its roots, and the final two to four weeks of swell before harvest, when most of the fruit's size is set. Water stress in that final swell causes irreversible loss of size and quality, so soak deeply at the root zone and let the surface dry between waterings rather than sprinkling lightly.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: In a dry spell, deep and steady watering matters most at two times: a young tree in its first year putting down roots, and the final stretch as the fruit fills out before harvest. Let the tree go dry while the peaches are sizing and they will stay small for the season, so give a deep soak at the ground and let the top dry out between waterings instead of watering a little every day.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot spell, shade exposed peaches
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Peaches take summer heat well, but fruit on the sun-exposed side of the tree can sunburn during an extreme heat spell, showing as tan, sunken patches that later rot. Keep the tree well watered so it is not also drought-stressed, and avoid stripping interior leaves that shade fruit when you thin. A little canopy over the fruit is protection, not crowding.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Peaches handle summer heat well, but during an extreme hot spell the fruit on the sunny side can sunburn, showing as tan, sunken spots that may rot later. Keep the tree watered so heat and dryness are not hitting it at once, and when you thin, leave the leaves that shade the fruit. A bit of leaf cover over the peaches protects them.

planting.text_seasoned: Set the graft union two to three inches above the final soil line. Burying it lets the scion root and defeats the rootstock you chose.
planting.text_beginner: Keep the graft joint (where your variety meets its rootstock) two to three inches above the soil. If you bury it, the top can grow its own roots and you lose the benefit of the rootstock.
planting.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

planting.text_seasoned: Plant in full sun on a well-drained site. Peaches will not tolerate wet feet, and low frost-pocket sites lose early bloom to late frosts.
planting.text_beginner: Plant where the tree gets full sun and the soil drains well. Peaches hate soggy roots, and a low spot where cold air settles will lose the early flowers to late frost.
planting.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

establishment.text_seasoned: Remove every blossom the first year. A first-year tree that fruits diverts energy from root and scaffold development it cannot get back.
establishment.text_beginner: Pick off all the flowers the first year. If a brand-new tree fruits, it spends energy it needs for roots and branches, and it cannot make that up.
establishment.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

establishment.text_seasoned: The first season is the tree's most water-sensitive period; water deeply and regularly so roots establish before the tree is left to rainfall.
establishment.text_beginner: Water deeply and often all through the first season. A new tree needs steady water to get its roots going before you can rely on rain.
establishment.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

first_growth.text_seasoned: Begin light formative pruning as new shoots extend, steering toward an open-center framework early rather than correcting a crowded tree later.
first_growth.text_beginner: As new shoots grow, start light pruning to guide the tree toward an open, vase-like shape. Shaping it early is far easier than fixing a crowded tree later.
first_growth.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

dormancy.text_seasoned: Winter chill is banking next year's bloom. Match your variety's chill requirement to what your winters actually deliver; a high-chill variety in a mild winter blooms poorly.
dormancy.text_beginner: The cold of winter is what sets up next spring's flowers. Pick a variety whose chill needs match your winters. A high-chill variety in a mild-winter area will barely bloom.
dormancy.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

dormancy.text_seasoned: Clear mummified fruit and fallen debris over winter. These are the overwintering sources of brown rot and other disease for the coming season.
dormancy.text_beginner: Clear away any dried-up mummy fruit and fallen debris during winter. These carry brown rot and other diseases into the next season.
dormancy.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Peaches are pruned harder than most fruit trees and bear on one-year-old wood, so annual renewal pruning is essential, not optional, for a continued crop.
dormant_prune.text_beginner: Peaches get pruned harder than most fruit trees, and they fruit on wood that grew last year. So pruning every year is a must, not a maybe, if you want a crop.
dormant_prune.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Make clean cuts and remove cankered wood. Ragged wounds and cankers are exactly what draw peachtree and lesser peachtree borers.
dormant_prune.text_beginner: Make clean cuts and remove any dead, sunken cankered bark. Ragged wounds and cankers are just what attract the borers.
dormant_prune.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

blossom.text_seasoned: Open bloom is the most frost-vulnerable moment of the year. Track the forecast, and cover a small tree overnight if a hard late frost threatens the flowers.
blossom.text_beginner: When the tree is in full bloom it is most at risk from frost. Watch the forecast, and if a hard late frost is coming, cover a small tree overnight to protect the flowers.
blossom.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

blossom.text_seasoned: Most peaches are self-fertile, so a single tree sets fruit alone. A few recommended varieties (notably J.H. Hale) are not, and need a second peach blooming at the same time.
blossom.text_beginner: Most peaches are self-fertile, so one tree fruits on its own. A few varieties, like J.H. Hale, are not, and need a second peach blooming nearby at the same time.
blossom.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Thin young fruit to one peach every 6 to 8 inches. Thinning is the single biggest lever on fruit size and the main protection against limb breakage.
fruit_set.text_beginner: Thin the little peaches to about one every 6 to 8 inches along the branch. Thinning does more for fruit size than anything else, and it keeps branches from breaking.
fruit_set.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Thin while fruit is still small, and take off insect-scarred fruit as you go. Early removal of plum-curculio-marked fruit also lowers next year's pressure.
fruit_set.text_beginner: Thin while the fruit is small, and remove any with insect scars as you go. Taking off the curculio-marked peaches early also means fewer beetles next year.
fruit_set.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

harvest.text_seasoned: A tree ripens over one to two weeks; pick in several passes. Ripe fruit loses its green undertone, gives slightly, and pulls free with a gentle twist.
harvest.text_beginner: The tree ripens over one to two weeks, so pick it a few times. A ripe peach has lost its green tinge, gives a little when squeezed, and twists off easily.
harvest.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

harvest.text_seasoned: Handle gently. Bruises are entry points for brown rot, and tree-ripe peaches are fragile; cool the fruit promptly if not eaten soon.
harvest.text_beginner: Handle the fruit gently. Bruises let brown rot in, and fully ripe peaches are delicate. Chill them soon if you are not eating them right away.
harvest.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

post_harvest.text_seasoned: Clear all remaining and dropped fruit after harvest. Fruit left to mummify on the tree or ground is the primary brown-rot inoculum for next year.
post_harvest.text_beginner: After harvest, clear every leftover and dropped peach. Fruit left to dry into mummies on the tree or ground is the main source of brown rot next year.
post_harvest.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

post_harvest.text_seasoned: Late summer is the window for a protective borer trunk inspection. Check the soil line for fresh gum and frass so a first-year infestation is caught early.
post_harvest.text_beginner: Late summer is a good time to check the base of the trunk for borers. Look at the soil line for fresh gummy ooze and sawdust-like frass so you catch them in the first year.
post_harvest.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A mature standard-rootstock peach (roughly years 4 and up) commonly yields about 1 to 3 bushels per tree, on the order of 50 to 150 pounds, depending on variety, pruning, thinning, and season. Crop is far more limited by thinning and frost than by feeding, so a properly thinned tree carries fewer but much larger, sweeter fruit.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: A grown peach tree on a standard rootstock (about year 4 onward) usually gives roughly 50 to 150 pounds of fruit a year, which is a lot of peaches. The exact amount depends on the variety, how you prune and thin, and the weather. Remember that thinning off the extra little peaches gives you fewer but much bigger and sweeter ones.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Trees reach full bearing around years 4 to 6 and stay productive for many years after, given annual pruning, thinning, and disease control. Peak per-tree yield depends heavily on training to an open center so light reaches all the fruiting wood.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: A peach tree hits its full fruit production around years 4 to 6 and keeps producing for years after that, as long as you prune, thin, and manage diseases each year. Keeping the tree pruned to an open vase shape, so sunlight reaches all the branches, makes a big difference in how much it bears.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Expect no crop in the planting year and little to none in year 2. Remove any fruit that sets early so the tree puts its energy into roots and a strong scaffold; the first meaningful harvest typically comes in year 3, with full bearing by years 4 to 6.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Do not expect peaches the first year, or really the second. If a few fruit form early, pick them off so the young tree can build roots and strong branches instead. Your first real harvest usually comes in year 3, with full crops by years 4 to 6.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No moon-phase planting preference is asserted. Extension sources do not support timing peach planting or care by lunar phase; site, chill matching, and frost avoidance govern outcomes.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Tree bloomed but set little or no fruit
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The tree flowered but I got almost no peaches
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The tree flowered well but few or no peaches formed. The most common cause on peach is a late frost during or just after bloom, which kills the open flowers and tiny fruit; in mild-winter areas, too few chill hours can also produce weak, uneven bloom that sets poorly. It is often blamed on a pollination failure, but most peaches are self-fertile and a lone tree should set fruit on its own. The fix is site and variety: avoid frost-pocket planting sites, protect bloom from hard late frosts where you can, and match the variety's chill requirement to your winters.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The tree flowered but barely fruited. On peaches the usual reason is a late frost while the tree was blooming, which kills the flowers and tiny fruit. In mild-winter areas, too little winter cold (chill hours) can also give a weak bloom that does not set. People often think the tree needed a pollinator partner, but most peaches are self-fertile and one tree should fruit by itself. The real fixes are where and what you plant: avoid low frost-pocket spots, cover the tree against a hard late frost when you can, and pick a variety whose chill needs match your winters.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Choose a frost-aware site, keep a frost cover ready for bloom, and confirm your variety's chill requirement suits your region before relying on it for a crop.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant away from low frost pockets, keep a cover handy for bloom-time frosts, and make sure your variety's chill needs fit your area before counting on a crop.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Spring leaves are thick, curled, and reddened
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: New spring leaves are puckered, curled, and red
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Newly emerged spring leaves are thickened, puckered, curled, and flushed red to purple. This is peach leaf curl, caused by the fungus Taphrina deformans, which infects the young leaves as buds swell in cool, wet spring weather. Growers often reach for a spray once they see it, but no spray cures curled leaves; the infection is already complete. The only effective control is a dormant fungicide applied on the leafless tree, so the real action belongs to next dormancy, not this spring. Keep the tree watered and fed to carry it through the season.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The new spring leaves are thick, puckered, curled, and red or purple. This is peach leaf curl, a fungus (Taphrina deformans) that infects the young leaves as the buds swell in cool, wet spring weather. Many people try to spray when they see it, but no spray fixes the curled leaves; the damage is already done. The only thing that works is a dormant spray on the bare, leafless tree, so the real fix is next winter, not now. Keep the tree watered and fed to get it through the year.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Apply a fixed-copper dormant spray on the leafless tree, timed for after about 90 percent leaf fall in autumn or just before bud swell in late winter, every year in leaf-curl-prone areas.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Spray fixed copper on the bare tree while it is dormant, in fall after most leaves drop or in late winter just before the buds swell, every year if leaf curl is common where you live.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The tree carried a heavy crop of small, poorly flavored fruit. Peaches characteristically overset, and an unthinned tree divides its resources among too many fruit. It is easy to assume the tree needs more feeding or water, but the limiting factor is fruit number, not inputs; an overloaded tree also risks limb breakage. The corrective action is thinning: remove young fruit early to about one peach every 6 to 8 inches so the remainder size and sweeten properly.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The tree had lots of small, bland peaches. Peaches naturally set far more fruit than they can size, and a tree that is not thinned splits its energy among too many. It is tempting to think it needs more food or water, but the real problem is too many peaches, not too few inputs, and an overloaded branch can even break. The fix is thinning: remove the small fruit early down to about one every 6 to 8 inches so the rest grow large and sweet.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Thin young fruit early and firmly to one peach every 6 to 8 inches; this single step does more for size and flavor than feeding or watering.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Thin the small fruit early to about one every 6 to 8 inches. This one step does more for size and taste than extra food or water.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Gummy ooze and frass at the base of the trunk
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Sticky gum and sawdust at the bottom of the trunk
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Gummy ooze mixed with sawdust-like frass has appeared at the soil line, sometimes with a mounded look. This is the signature of peachtree borer, whose larvae tunnel in the inner bark at the crown. Peaches gum in response to many stresses, so the ooze alone is sometimes dismissed as harmless sap; the frass is the tell that larvae are inside, and a young tree can be girdled and killed. The corrective action is to expose the crown, locate the entry holes, and kill the larvae by hand, then protect the trunk base from the wounds that attract egg-laying.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Sticky gum mixed with what looks like wet sawdust (frass) has shown up where the trunk meets the soil, sometimes in a little mound. This is the sign of peachtree borer, whose larvae tunnel in the bark at the base. Peaches ooze gum for many reasons, so it is easy to shrug off as ordinary sap, but the sawdusty frass means larvae are inside, and they can kill a young tree. The fix is to scrape away the soil, find the holes, and kill the larvae with a wire, then keep the trunk base free of the wounds that draw the moths.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Inspect the soil line each late summer for fresh gum and frass, keep mowers and trimmers off the trunk base, and worm out any larvae promptly before they girdle the tree.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Check the base of the trunk every late summer for fresh gum and frass, keep mowers and trimmers away from it, and dig out any larvae right away before they ring the trunk.

succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Succession planting does not apply to peach. It is a permanent tree that occupies its site for many years and bears once each season as the fruit ripens, so there is no staggered re-sowing to schedule the way there is for a short-season annual crop.

open_findings.summary: rotation dict is annual-shaped (rotation_years/avoid_after/good_after); authored honestly for a permanent tree (rotation_years:null + the replant-disease angle), but a perennial-aware variant (rotation_applicable:false / replant_disease_*) is owed in the tree spec before apple so the renderer does not imply a rotation interval.

3.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 3 winter lows (down to -40°F) are below the survival threshold of even the hardiest peach cultivars; the tree is likely to be killed outright. Not a peach zone.
3.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 3 is too cold for peach trees to survive. This is not a peach-growing zone.

4.suitability_note_seasoned: The hardiest cultivars (Reliance, Contender) can survive zone 4, but fruit buds die between -13°F and -18°F and late frosts hit the early bloom, so a reliable crop does not happen here. The tree may set fruit in a rare mild year, but it is often short-lived and should be treated as a tree that survives rather than one that crops.
4.suitability_note_beginner: A very hardy peach variety may survive here, but you should not count on peaches. The tree usually lives only a handful of years and rarely fruits. Treat zone 4 as too cold for dependable peaches.
4.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Late spring frosts are the defining risk here: even the hardiest, latest-blooming cultivars (Reliance, Contender, Intrepid) open their flowers in May, and a single hard freeze on the open bloom takes that year's crop. Fruit buds also die between -13°F and -18°F in deep winter. Expect the tree to bloom most springs but to set a usable crop only in the years that escape a killing frost.

5.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 5 is the marginal lower edge of reliable peach fruiting. The hardiest late-blooming cultivars crop in good years on frost-safe sites; a hard midwinter cold snap or a late spring frost can still take a season. Favor Reliance and Contender and avoid low, frost-prone ground.
5.suitability_note_beginner: Peaches can fruit in zone 5 in good years if you choose a cold-hardy variety and plant on high, open ground. Some years a late frost or deep cold will cost you the crop.
5.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Late spring frost on the open bloom is the main crop risk. Choose late-blooming cultivars and frost-safe sites to dodge most freezes.

6.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 6 is reliable peach country with chill to spare, so the full variety range is open; pick by flavor and ripening season. Watch the occasional late frost on early bloomers, but most years crop well.
6.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 6 grows peaches dependably. You can choose almost any variety. Just keep an eye out for a late frost when the tree is in bloom.
6.frost_risk_note_seasoned: An occasional late-April frost can nip the earliest bloomers; mid-to-late-blooming cultivars are the safer choice.

7.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 7 fruits peaches reliably across the full variety range; chill is ample and the season is long. Late frost risk is modest. Choose by ripening sequence to spread the harvest.
7.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 7 is excellent for peaches. Almost any variety works, and the growing season is long enough for a good crop.
7.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Late-frost loss is occasional and falls hardest on the very-early bloomers; a mid-to-late cultivar is the lower-risk pick.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the north, peaches do best in the milder parts (zones 6 and 7). Farther north the tree may live but give fruit only some years. Plant on higher ground away from the coldest low spots, and choose a cold-hardy variety.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Across the northern tier, peach success is set by how cold your winter gets and how late your spring frosts run, not by chill. Reliable cropping starts around zone 6; zones 3 to 5 ask for the hardiest cultivars, careful frost-pocket avoidance, and patience with off years.
northern_tier.chill_basis_seasoned: Northern-tier winters bank well over 1,000 chill hours, far more than any peach variety needs, so chill is never the limiter here. The limits are cold and frost: midwinter lows damage fruit buds (below about -13°F to -18°F) and a late spring frost can kill an open bloom.
northern_tier.chill_basis_beginner: Winters here are plenty cold for any peach variety. The challenge is not too little cold, it is too much: deep winter cold and late spring frosts are what threaten the crop.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Reliable peach country. Choose cultivars in the roughly 650 to 900 chill-hour range; inland zone 8 winters bank enough chill most years. Peak bloom falls in mid-March, so late-March frosts are the main threat to the crop.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Peaches grow very well here. Choose a mid-range variety and watch for a late frost in March when the tree blooms.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Bloom peaks in mid-March, and a late-March freeze can wipe out the early-blooming cultivars; favor mid-to-late bloom groups for security.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: The warm, lower-chill Gulf edge. Winters bank only about 500 to 650 chill hours, so favor lower-chill cultivars (around 500 to 600 hours); the high-chill set will not fruit reliably. Very early bloom raises frost exposure in cool springs.
9.suitability_note_beginner: This warmer edge can grow peaches, but only lower-chill varieties, and some winters are too mild for a full crop. Choose a low-chill variety.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Bloom comes very early here, so even a mild late freeze can catch open flowers. Lower-chill, slightly later cultivars reduce the risk.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: The Southeast grows wonderful peaches. Inland you can pick most varieties; near the warm coast, choose a low-chill variety. The main worry is a late frost in spring while the tree is blooming.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: This is classic peach country. Inland zone 8 sites crop the broad mid-chill range dependably; the warmer, lower-chill zone 9 edge near the coast needs lower-chill cultivars and still runs short some winters. Late-March and April frosts on the early bloom are the recurring crop risk.
se_gulf.chill_basis_seasoned: Southeastern winters bank roughly 600 to 1,000 chill hours inland, tapering toward the Gulf. Mid-chill to high-chill cultivars (around 650 to 900 hours) fruit reliably inland; very-low-chill types bloom too early and lose the crop to frost, while the highest-chill cultivars fall short in the warmer coastal edge.
se_gulf.chill_basis_beginner: Winters across the Southeast are usually cold enough for most peach varieties. Closer to the Gulf coast, choose a lower-chill variety; inland, most varieties do well.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Prime peach country with ample chill; the full variety range is open. Choose by ripening season to spread a long harvest. Frost risk is low but not zero in cold valley pockets.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Excellent for peaches. Almost any variety works, with a long picking season through summer.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: A late-February or March frost can occasionally catch the earliest bloom in cold valley pockets; mid-season cultivars are the safer pick on frosty sites.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Lower Central Valley zone 9 still banks high chill in most winters and crops reliably; favor cultivars around 700 to 900 hours as a hedge against the warmest winters. Bloom is early and the harvest runs long.
9.suitability_note_beginner: This part of the valley grows peaches well. Choose a mid-range variety to be safe in a mild winter, and enjoy a long summer harvest.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Early bloom means a late freeze can occasionally reach open flowers in low-lying ground; a mid-season cultivar trims the risk.

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: Interior California is one of the best places to grow peaches. Most varieties do well here, with an early bloom and a long summer harvest.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: Prime stone-fruit country. Both zones crop the broad variety range reliably, with early bloom (late February to March) and a long harvest from May into August. Late frosts are infrequent but possible in the lower valley; chill adequacy is the variable to watch in warm winters.
ca_interior.chill_basis_seasoned: Interior California (the Central Valley) banks roughly 700 to 1,100 chill hours in a typical winter, enough for the broad mid-to-high-chill range. Chill totals have trended downward in mild years, so leaning toward cultivars near 700 to 900 hours hedges against a warm winter.
ca_interior.chill_basis_beginner: The Central Valley usually gets enough winter cold for most peach varieties. In a mild winter, a mid-range variety is the safer choice.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Inland north-coast valleys bank a declining 400 to 800 chill hours; mid-low-chill cultivars fruit in good years, the high-chill set does not. Favor cultivars at or below your typical local chill, and expect short winters to thin the crop.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Peaches can fruit here in good years if you pick a low-chill variety. Mild winters will sometimes mean a light crop.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is a minor risk on the mild coast; the real limit is whether the winter banks enough chill for the variety you chose.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: Cooler coastal zone 10 banks low chill, often under 500 hours, so only the lowest-chill cultivars (around 400 hours, such as Florida King) are worth trying, and many winters fall short. The tree grows easily; the crop is the gamble.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Right on the coast, winters are usually too mild for a full crop. Only the lowest-chill varieties have a chance, and even those miss some years.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Late frost is rarely the problem on the coast; short winter chill is what limits fruit set here.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: Near the Northern California coast, winters are mild. Pick a low-chill peach variety, and expect better crops a bit inland than right on the coast.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: Mild maritime winters make chill adequacy the deciding factor. Inland zone 9 valleys bank enough for mid-low-chill cultivars; the cooler, lower-chill coastal zone 10 only suits low-chill types and falls short in warm winters. Frost risk is low; the limit is chill, not cold.
ca_north_coast.chill_basis_seasoned: North-coast California winters are mild and bank only about 400 to 800 chill hours, and the totals have been declining. Lower-chill and mid-chill cultivars fruit; the high-chill set is unreliable here, and warm-winter daytime temperatures above about 65°F can erode the running chill total.
ca_north_coast.chill_basis_beginner: Coastal Northern California has mild winters that may not give enough cold for every peach variety. Choose a low-chill or mid-chill variety for the best results.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Cooler, slightly inland south-coast sites bank about 200 to 500 chill hours, enough for the lowest-chill cultivars in good years only. Florida King's roughly 400-hour need sits near the top of what these winters deliver, so crops are light and inconsistent.
9.suitability_note_beginner: In the cooler inland parts of the Southern California coast, a low-chill peach may fruit in good years, but crops will be small and not every year.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is seldom the issue here; the shortfall is winter chill, which leaves blossoms dropping without setting fruit in mild years.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: The warmest south-coast zone 10 sites bank under about 300 chill hours most winters, below even Florida King's roughly 400-hour requirement. The tree grows and survives easily, but the blossoms drop without setting a reliable crop. Of the cultivars here, none is low-chill enough for dependable fruit.
10.suitability_note_beginner: In the warmest coastal areas, winters are too mild for these peach varieties to fruit. The tree will grow happily but give little or no fruit.

ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: Along the Southern California coast, winters are too mild for most peaches. A low-chill variety might fruit in the cooler inland spots, but in the warmest coastal areas the tree will grow without giving much fruit.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: Chill scarcity defines this region. Slightly inland and cooler zone 9 sites suit low-chill cultivars marginally; the warmest coastal zone 10 sites usually cannot bank even the roughly 400 hours the lowest-chill cultivar here needs, so the tree survives but rarely fruits. Heat and survival are never the issue; chill is.
ca_south_coast.chill_basis_seasoned: Southern-coast California winters are very mild and bank only about 200 to 500 chill hours; coastal stations such as San Luis Obispo run near 230 hours. Only low-chill cultivars have a chance, and the lowest-chill coastal sites fall short of even Florida King's roughly 400-hour need most years.
ca_south_coast.chill_basis_beginner: The Southern California coast has very mild winters with little cold. Only low-chill peach varieties may fruit, and right on the coast even those often will not get enough cold.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 desert sites bank about 300 to 400 chill hours, just enough for a low-chill cultivar near 400 hours (such as Florida King) in cooler winters. Choose the lowest-chill, earliest-ripening cultivar so fruit matures before summer heat; expect light crops in warm winters.
9.suitability_note_beginner: A low-chill peach may fruit here in cooler winters. Pick the lowest-chill, earliest variety so the fruit ripens before the summer gets too hot.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: An early bloom can meet a late desert frost in cool years; otherwise the binding limit is short winter chill.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: The hottest, lowest-chill desert sites bank under about 300 chill hours, below even the lowest-chill cultivar here. The tree survives the heat but the crop does not set. Extreme summer temperatures further stress any fruit that does form.
10.suitability_note_beginner: The hottest desert spots stay too warm in winter for these peaches to set fruit, and the fierce summer heat works against them too. Expect a living tree but little or no fruit here.

ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: In the California desert, winters are too mild for most peaches and summers are very hot. Choose the lowest-chill, earliest variety you can find so the fruit ripens before the heat. In the hottest spots the tree may grow but not fruit.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: A very-low-chill region where only the lowest-chill, earliest-ripening, self-fruitful cultivars fit, and fruit must ripen before the brutal summer heat. Zone 9 sites marginally bank enough for a cultivar near 400 hours; the hottest zone 10 sites usually do not, leaving a surviving tree that does not crop.
ca_desert.chill_basis_seasoned: Low-desert California winters bank only about 250 to 400 chill hours, with most accumulation in December and January and warm days subtracting from the total. Only sub-400-hour low-chill cultivars are viable, and the hottest, lowest-chill sites fall below even that.
ca_desert.chill_basis_beginner: The California desert has very mild winters with little cold. Only the lowest-chill peach varieties have a chance, and in the hottest spots even those may not get enough cold to fruit.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Reliable peach country when matched to chill. Choose cultivars around 450 to 650 chill hours (Florida King at 450, the Texas mid-chill types at 550 to 600); higher-chill cultivars are a gamble in warm winters. Late frost after the early bloom is the main crop risk.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Peaches grow well here with a mid-range variety. The biggest risk is a late frost in spring after the tree has bloomed.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: A late freeze after the early bloom is the classic crop-killer here; a couple of below-freezing nights on open flowers can take most of the fruit. Favor mid-to-late bloom groups.

warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: This warm, dry region grows good peaches. Choose a mid-range variety and watch for a late spring frost after the tree blooms, which is the main thing that costs a crop.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: Established peach country with variable chill. Choose cultivars around 450 to 650 hours for dependable cropping; the recurring threat is a late freeze after an early bloom, which can erase a season. Harvest runs from May through August across the variety range.
warm_arid.chill_basis_seasoned: Inland warm-arid winters (the Texas Hill Country and similar) bank roughly 450 to 850 chill hours in a typical year, though warm winters can fall to the 500s. Mid-chill cultivars (around 450 to 650 hours) fruit reliably; higher-chill types are marginal in warm winters, when trees leaf out slowly and shed blossoms.
warm_arid.chill_basis_beginner: Winters here are usually cold enough for mid-range peach varieties, but a warm winter can mean a light crop. A mid-chill or low-chill variety is the safer choice.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Low-desert zone 9 banks about 300 to 400 chill hours, so only the lowest-chill cultivar here (Florida King at 400 hours) fits, and only marginally in cooler winters. Plant bare-root in January, choose an early ripener, and expect a crop that finishes before summer heat. Higher-chill cultivars will not fruit.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Only the lowest-chill peach varieties can fruit in the Arizona low desert, and even those miss in warm winters. Plant in winter and pick before the summer heat.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: An early bloom can occasionally meet a late desert frost; more often the binding limit is whether the winter banked the 400 chill hours the variety needs.

low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: In the Arizona low desert, pick the lowest-chill, earliest peach variety. Plant it bare-root in winter and you can harvest in late spring before the heat. Most standard varieties will not get enough winter cold to fruit here.
low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: A low-chill region where the recipe is fixed: low-chill (under 400 hours), early-maturing, self-fruitful cultivars, planted bare-root in January, ripening late May to June ahead of the heat. Of the cultivars here, only Florida King at 400 hours fits, and then only marginally in cooler winters.
low_desert_az.chill_basis_seasoned: Low-desert Arizona winters bank about 300 to 400 chill hours, counted between November 1 and February 15, with most benefit in December and January and warm days above about 60°F subtracting. Only sub-400-hour low-chill cultivars are viable, and the crop must ripen before the summer heat.
low_desert_az.chill_basis_beginner: The Arizona low desert has mild winters with little cold. Choose the lowest-chill, earliest peach variety you can, so the fruit ripens before the desert summer arrives.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: Central-peninsula zone 10 banks roughly 150 to 350 chill hours, below the roughly 400 hours the lowest-chill cultivar in this set needs. The tree grows in Florida's warmth, but these cultivars drop their blossoms without setting fruit. Florida-adapted UF cultivars (100 to 200 hours), not listed here, are the ones that crop in this zone.
10.suitability_note_beginner: In the central Florida peninsula, the peach varieties listed here will not get enough winter cold to fruit. The tree may grow, but it will not give peaches. Only special low-chill Florida varieties fruit here.

11.suitability_note_seasoned: South-peninsula zone 11 banks almost no chill (under about 150 hours), far below any cultivar in this set. Peaches will not fruit; the climate simply does not deliver the winter cold the trees require.
11.suitability_note_beginner: South Florida is too warm in winter for peaches to fruit. These varieties need cold the area does not get.

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: The Florida peninsula is too warm in winter for the peach varieties listed here. There are special low-chill Florida peaches bred by the University of Florida, but they are not in this set. For these varieties, the peninsula will not give fruit.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: The honesty of the model shows here: of this variety set, none is low-chill enough for the peninsula. The University of Florida breeds peninsula-adapted cultivars at 100 to 200 chill hours, but those sit outside this list, so for the cultivars here the peninsula reads as no reliable crop (central) to genuinely unsuitable (south).
fl_peninsula.chill_basis_seasoned: The Florida peninsula banks very little winter chill, accumulating only from October into early January and falling well below 350 hours in the central peninsula and near zero in the south. Standard peach cultivars cannot meet their chill requirement here; only the specialized University of Florida low-chill cultivars (100 to 200 hours) fruit, and none of those are in this variety set.
fl_peninsula.chill_basis_beginner: The Florida peninsula has warm winters with almost no cold. Standard peach varieties will not fruit here. Special Florida-bred low-chill peaches exist, but the varieties listed here need more winter cold than the peninsula provides.

11.suitability_note_seasoned: Hawaii banks effectively zero chill, far below the requirement of any peach cultivar. Peaches will not fruit; this is a genuine no-grow case, not a marginal one.
11.suitability_note_beginner: Peaches need cold winters to fruit, and Hawaii does not have them. Peaches will not grow fruit here.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: Peaches need a cold winter to fruit, and Hawaii does not have one. Peaches will not produce here.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: Hawaii is the clearest case of the model telling the truth instead of inventing a window: peaches need a cold winter to fruit, and Hawaii has none. The verdict is simply unsuitable, with no fabricated planting calendar.
hawaii_tropical.chill_basis_seasoned: Hawaii's tropical winters deliver essentially no chill (well under 100 hours), because temperatures rarely fall into the 32°F to 45°F range that counts. Peaches require accumulated winter chill to break dormancy and bloom, and that requirement cannot be met here for any cultivar.
hawaii_tropical.chill_basis_beginner: Hawaii does not get cold winters, so peach trees never get the chill they need to make fruit.

crops.description_seasoned: Peach is a deciduous stone-fruit tree (Prunus persica) prized for fruit that ripens best tree-ripened in the home garden, where it can hang to full flavor rather than being picked firm for shipping. It is self-fertile, so a single tree bears, but it asks for real commitment: an annual dormant pruning to an open-center vase, a disciplined spray program against brown rot and insects, early fruit thinning, and a planting site chosen to dodge late-frost pockets. A peach also needs enough winter chill to break dormancy evenly, so variety choice is matched to your winters. Given that care, a backyard tree rewards you with fruit grocery shelves cannot match.
crops.description_beginner: A peach is a fruit tree that drops its leaves each winter and gives you fruit you can let ripen right on the branch, which is where peaches taste their best. One tree fruits on its own, so you do not need a second one to get peaches. Peaches do take steady work, though: you prune the tree every winter into an open vase shape, spray on a schedule to keep fruit diseases and bugs in check, thin off the extra little fruit so the rest grow big, and plant where late spring frosts are less likely to settle. Peaches also need a cold-enough winter to wake up and bloom evenly, so you pick a variety that fits your area. With that care, a backyard peach gives you fruit far better than the store.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: A peach is ready when the ground color (the background skin under the red blush) shifts from green to a warm yellow or cream, the flesh gives slightly to gentle pressure near the stem, the aroma turns full and sweet, and the fruit separates from the spur with a light upward twist. Red blush alone is not ripeness; it is driven by sun and variety. Pick when fully colored but still firm if you need to handle or store the fruit, and let it finish on the counter; pick at full give for eating that day.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: A peach is ripe when the background skin color (the part under the red) turns from green to a warm yellow or cream, the fruit gives a little when you press gently near the stem, it smells sweet and peachy, and it comes off the branch with a gentle twist instead of a hard pull. The red color by itself does not mean ripe, since that comes from sun and the variety. If you need to carry or store them, pick when fully colored but still firm and let them soften on the counter. For eating right away, pick when they give to a gentle squeeze.
crops.bloom_time_seasoned: Peaches bloom in early spring, typically late February through April depending on region, chill accumulation, and variety, often before the leaves fully expand. Bloom timing is variety-driven: low-chill types like Florida King open very early, while higher-chill standards like Cresthaven bloom later. Early bloom is the tree's chief vulnerability, since open flowers are killed by hard late frosts.
crops.bloom_time_beginner: Peach trees flower in early spring, usually sometime from late February to April depending on where you live and the variety, often before the leaves are fully out. Some varieties bloom very early and others later. Early flowers are the tree's weak point, because a hard late frost can kill the open blooms and the tiny fruit behind them.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Peach trees survive winters across zones 4 to 9, but surviving is not the same as fruiting. The tree itself is hardy to roughly -20°F; below that the wood is damaged, and around -25°F the tree can be killed. The fruit buds are the weak link: they begin to die between -13°F and -18°F, so the reliable-fruit band is narrower than the survival band. Peaches fruit most dependably in zones 6 to 8. Zone 5 is a marginal lower edge where only the hardiest late-blooming cultivars (Reliance, Contender) crop in good years, and then only on sites that escape the coldest air. The warm edge near zone 9 is limited not by cold but by winter chill: where winters no longer bank enough chill hours, even a thriving tree blooms poorly and sets little fruit.
crops.hardiness_notes_beginner: Peach trees can live in zones 4 through 9, but living and fruiting are two different things. The tree is tough, yet its flower buds are not. You will get the most dependable peaches in zones 6, 7, and 8. In colder spots (zones 4 and 5) the tree may survive but rarely give a full crop, and in the warmest spots the winters can be too mild for the tree to fruit well. Pick a variety suited to your zone and you give yourself the best odds.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Peaches need a stretch of winter cold, counted as chill hours (hours between 32°F and 45°F), to break dormancy and bloom evenly. The requirement is set by the variety, not the species: the cultivars here span about 400 chill hours (Florida King, a low-chill type) to 1,050 (Contender, a high-chill type). Match the variety to the chill your winters actually bank. Too few chill hours and the blossoms drop without setting fruit; warm winter days above about 65°F can subtract from the running total.
crops.chill_hours_note_beginner: Peach trees need enough cold winter hours, called chill hours, before they will bloom properly in spring. Different varieties need different amounts. If your winters are mild, choose a low-chill variety; if your winters are cold, you can grow almost any variety. Planting a high-chill variety where winters are warm usually means lots of leaves and very few peaches.
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Most peaches are self-fertile, so a single tree sets a full crop on its own without a pollinizer partner; this is the inverse of many apples, which require cross-pollination. The notable exception among recommended varieties is J.H. Hale, which is not self-fertile and needs a second peach blooming at the same time nearby. Peaches are insect-pollinated, mainly by bees, so supporting pollinator activity at bloom helps fruit set even on a lone self-fertile tree.
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: Most peaches are self-fertile, which means one tree makes peaches by itself with no second tree needed. This is different from many apples, which do need a partner tree. The main exception is the variety J.H. Hale, which is not self-fertile and needs another peach blooming nearby at the same time. Bees do the pollinating, so anything that helps bees be active during bloom helps your tree set fruit, even a single self-fertile one.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: In the planting year, prioritize establishment over fruit. Plant a dormant bare-root tree in late winter, head it back at planting to begin the open-center scaffold, keep a weed-free, mulched circle around the trunk, and water consistently through the first two seasons. Remove any fruit that sets. Hold fertilizer until growth begins, and never feed late in the season.
crops.year_one_notes_beginner: The first year is about helping the tree settle in, not getting fruit. Plant a bare-root tree in late winter while it is still dormant, cut it back at planting to start the open vase shape, keep a mulched, weed-free ring around the trunk, and water it steadily through the first couple of seasons. Pull off any fruit that forms. Wait to fertilize until the tree starts growing, and never feed late in the year.

pollination.notes_seasoned: Self-fertile: a single tree fruits without a pollinizer. Exception: J.H. Hale requires a compatible second peach blooming concurrently. Bees are the primary pollinators; ensure bloom-time pollinator activity for reliable set.
pollination.notes_beginner: Self-fertile means one tree fruits on its own, no second tree required. The one common exception is J.H. Hale, which needs another peach blooming nearby at the same time. Bees do the work, so good bee activity during bloom helps the tree set a full crop.

crops.establishment_note: Most peaches begin bearing about 3 years after planting.
crops.recommended_rootstock_note: Pick a rootstock for your soil and pests, not for tree size; peach rootstocks do not make the tree smaller.

rootstock_options.name: Lovell
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask for your variety on Lovell for heavier, well-drained soils.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: Standard-size seedling rootstock and the long-time benchmark. Tolerant of peach tree short life and suited to heavier, well-drained soils, but susceptible to root-knot nematode and weaker on replant sites. A solid default where nematode pressure is low.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: A full-size, traditional rootstock that does well in heavier soils and resists a problem called peach tree short life, but it is not the best where soil-dwelling nematode pests are present. A good standard choice if your soil does not have nematode trouble.

rootstock_options.name: Halford
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask for Halford for heavier soils where ring nematodes are not a problem.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: Standard seedling rootstock similar in stature to Lovell, well-suited to heavier soils where ring nematodes are not a concern. Like Lovell, it lacks strong nematode resistance, so it is best matched to sites without that pressure.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: A full-size rootstock much like Lovell, good for heavier soils as long as nematodes are not a problem in your ground. It is not the one to pick where those soil pests are present.

rootstock_options.name: Guardian
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask for Guardian on sandy soils where ring nematodes and Peach Tree Short Life occur.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: Standard-size rootstock released by USDA-ARS and Clemson, bred for the Southeast. Its standout trait is a combination of peach tree short life resistance and root-knot nematode resistance, giving excellent survival on sandy southeastern sites where older rootstocks fail. The preferred choice where ring nematodes and short-life are present.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: A full-size rootstock developed for the Southeast that resists both a deadly problem called peach tree short life and soil nematode pests, so trees on it survive much better on sandy southern sites. This is the one to ask for where those soil problems exist.

rootstock_options.name: Nemaguard
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask for Nemaguard for sandy soils that need root-knot nematode resistance.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: Standard-size rootstock valued for strong root-knot nematode resistance and vigor on sandy, well-drained soils. Its weakness is susceptibility to peach tree short life, so it is best where nematodes are the main concern and short-life pressure is low; it also dislikes high-pH or saline soils.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: A full-size rootstock that strongly resists soil nematode pests and grows well in sandy, well-drained soil. Its downside is that it is prone to peach tree short life, so it fits best where nematodes are the worry rather than that disease.

crops.name: Apple

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Apple trees grow best in deep, rich soil that drains well, the kind of loamy soil that holds some moisture but never stays soggy. The one rule that matters most: the spot must drain. Apple roots rot if water sits around them, and that is the fastest way to lose a young tree. If your soil is heavy clay or stays wet, plant the tree on a low mound of soil instead of digging a deep hole, so water drains away from the roots.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Apple wants a deep, well-drained loam with steady moisture and moderate organic matter. The non-negotiable is drainage: apple roots will not tolerate standing water, and wet feet drive crown and root rots that kill young trees faster than any pest. On heavy clay or a high water table, plant on a raised berm or mound rather than amending the planting hole, which only makes a sump. Match the rootstock to the site as well, M9 and M26 dislike wet ground more than the more vigorous stocks do.

ph.note_beginner: Apple trees like soil that is slightly acidic, a pH around 6.0 to 6.5 (pH is just a measure of how acidic or alkaline soil is, where 7.0 is neutral). Test your soil before you plant, since it is much easier to fix the pH now than after the tree is in the ground. If the test says your soil is too acidic, garden lime raises the pH; if it is too alkaline, garden sulfur lowers it. Your local extension office can test a soil sample for you.
ph.note_seasoned: Apple does best at a slightly acidic pH of about 6.0 to 6.5, and tolerates roughly 5.5 to 7.0. Test the soil before planting and adjust the whole root zone, not just the hole, because correcting pH around an established tree is slow. Lime raises a low pH; elemental sulfur lowers a high one. Outside this band, iron and manganese become less available and you see interveinal yellowing on new growth even when those nutrients are present.

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Fertilize lightly in early spring before bud break, guided by shoot growth: a healthy young apple makes about 12 to 18 inches of new shoot growth per year, so feed to reach that, not beyond. Excess nitrogen drives soft, leafy growth that is highly susceptible to fire blight and delays fruiting. Mature trees on fertile soil often need little or no nitrogen.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Feed apple trees once a year, in early spring before the buds open, with a balanced fertilizer. Go easy: too much feeding makes lots of soft leaves instead of fruit and invites a serious disease called fire blight. If the tree is growing well and putting out healthy new branches each year, it may not need much at all.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced N-P-K ratio (the three numbers on the bag, nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium), such as 10-10-10, applied at a modest rate; lean toward lower nitrogen on vigorous trees to limit fire-blight-prone growth.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: The three numbers on a fertilizer bag are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. A balanced one like 10-10-10 is fine for apples. The first number (nitrogen) is the one to keep modest, too much makes the tree grow leaves instead of apples.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A common home rule is about 1/8 lb of actual nitrogen per year of tree age, capped near 1 lb actual N for a mature tree; always follow the product label and adjust down if annual shoot growth is already strong.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A simple guideline is a small amount that grows with the tree's age, following the directions on the fertilizer bag. When in doubt, use less, an underfed apple tree is healthier than an overfed one.

companions.note_beginner: Apples do not pair with other plants the way vegetables do. For an apple, the neighbor that counts is a second, different apple variety planted within about 50 ft that blooms at the same time, because most apple trees need another apple nearby to make fruit. Right around the trunk, do the opposite of planting companions: keep grass and other plants away from the base, out to the edge of the branches, because they steal water and food from the young tree. Use mulch there instead, and never plant an apple near a black walnut tree, which poisons the soil for apples.
companions.note_seasoned: Apple does not companion-plant in the vegetable sense; the interactions that actually matter are pollination and root competition. The single most important neighbor is a second, bloom-overlapping apple variety (the pollinizer) within about 50 ft, because nearly all apples are self-unfruitful. At the trunk, the rule is the reverse of companionship: keep turf and aggressive perennials out of the root zone, since grass competes hard with a young tree for water and nitrogen. Maintain a mulched, vegetation-free circle out to the dripline, and avoid siting near black walnut, whose juglone is toxic to apple.

pests.name: Codling moth
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Larvae tunnel into the fruit core, leaving a frass-filled entry hole (often at the calyx end) and brown trails; infested apples drop early or are inedible.
pests.symptoms_beginner: This is the classic "worm in the apple." You find a small hole in the apple with brown crumbly stuff (frass) around it, and a tunnel into the core when you cut it open. Bad apples drop early.
pests.cause_seasoned: Cydia pomonella; female moths lay eggs on developing fruit and young leaves near bloom, and hatching larvae bore into the apple. Two or more generations per season in most regions.
pests.cause_beginner: A small moth lays eggs on the tiny apples in spring; the eggs hatch into caterpillars that crawl into the fruit. There can be two batches a summer, so the problem repeats.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Monitor with pheromone traps to time control; remove and destroy dropped and infested fruit; bag individual fruit; spinosad or kaolin clay applied on a degree-day/petal-fall schedule. Mating disruption works at larger scale.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick up and throw away every apple that drops, do not leave them under the tree. You can slip paper bags or nylon footies over young apples to keep moths out, and traps with a moth scent help you know when to act. Sprays like spinosad work if timed right.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Orchard sanitation (clear dropped fruit and debris), keep nearby abandoned apple trees pruned or removed, and band trunks to catch larvae seeking pupation sites.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep the ground under the tree clean of fallen apples, and wrap a band of cardboard around the trunk to trap crawling caterpillars. Nearby neglected apple trees make it worse.

pests.name: Apple maggot
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Adult flies lay eggs under the skin; larvae tunnel through the flesh leaving dimpled, pitted fruit with brown winding trails inside.
