direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: In the California interior valleys (Sacramento, San Joaquin, and similar valleys), lettuce has a late-summer/early-fall window as peak summer heat begins to ease. The California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2 gives lettuce in the Interior Valleys as August, then again November through March. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program, Table 13.2) Sacramento County Master Gardeners note lettuce germinates poorly in warm summer soil because heat can cause seed dormancy, and bolts under high-temperature stress. (UC Master Gardeners of Sacramento County)

direct_sow.label: secondary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: The interior's main window is the mild winter into early spring (Table 13.2: November through March), a long cool-season window that opens after the first heat break and closes as returning spring heat triggers bolting. Harvest before sustained spring warmth. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program, Table 13.2)
direct_sow.design_note_seasoned: Winter-spring window anchored to the spring bolt close, working back across the Nov-Mar span; mild interior winters keep the window open throughout.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Late-summer-sown leaf lettuce in the interior reaches cut size in roughly 45 days under warm early-fall conditions; leaf types are at the fast end of the maturity range. Harvest single leaves as soon as they reach a usable size. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program)

harvest_start.label: secondary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Winter-sown leaf lettuce matures over roughly 50 to 60 days as cooler temperatures and shorter days slow growth relative to the late-summer window. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The interior lettuce season closes as returning spring heat drives bolting, turning leaves bitter and pushing a seed stalk. Harvest before sustained warm daytime temperatures. Sacramento County trials saw lettuce bolt during weeks of 106-107 degrees F. (UC Master Gardeners of Sacramento County; UC ANR Master Gardener Program)
harvest_end.design_note_seasoned: Conservative harvest_end: bolt_threshold_start - 5 days.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: May through July is excluded by interior-valley summer heat: lettuce germinates poorly in warm summer soil (heat-induced seed dormancy) and bolts under high-temperature stress. Sacramento County trials saw bolting in weeks of 106-107°F. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program; UC Master Gardeners of Sacramento County)

May through July is excluded by interior-valley summer heat: lettuce germinates poorly in warm summer soil (heat-induced seed dormancy) and bolts under high-temperature stress. Sacramento County trials saw bolting in weeks of 106-107°F. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program; UC Master Gardeners of Sacramento County)

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In the California interior valleys (Sacramento, San Joaquin, and nearby), lettuce grows in two stretches: a quick late-summer planting in August as the worst heat starts to ease, and a long main season from November through March over the mild winter. Skip the heart of summer (roughly May through July), when it is too hot, lettuce won't germinate well, and plants bolt and turn bitter. Harvest the winter crop before spring heat returns.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: Interior-valley calendar is heat-inverted with two windows (Table 13.2: August, then November through March). The August window is a short late-summer sowing as peak heat eases; the November-March window is the long mild-winter main season, closing as spring heat returns and drives bolting. Summer (roughly May through July) is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: lettuce germinates poorly in warm summer soil and bolts under high-temperature stress (Sacramento County trials bolted in weeks of 106-107°F). Frost is a minor secondary factor at the cooler zone-8 end. Windows verified against UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2, with UC Master Gardeners of Sacramento County corroboration for interior-valley heat behavior.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: On the California north coast and northern coastal interior (Monterey County north), lettuce is sown from late winter through summer; the cool, foggy maritime summer is the active growing season rather than an exclusion. The California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2 gives lettuce in the North and North Coast as February through August. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program, Table 13.2) Sow in late winter once the soil is workable and warming. The cold, wet winter, not summer heat, bounds the season here.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Leaf lettuce on the cool north coast reaches cut size in roughly 45 to 60 days; leaf types are at the fast end of the maturity range. The mild maritime summer keeps the crop productive across the season. Harvest single leaves as soon as they reach a usable size. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The north-coast lettuce season runs through summer and closes as the cool, wet winter sets in. Lettuce tolerates light frost but is bounded by the cold, damp end of the year rather than by summer heat. Harvest before extended cold and wet weather. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program, Table 13.2)
harvest_end.design_note_seasoned: Cool-limited region: season bounded by the cold/wet winter end (first_frost - 5), not by a spring bolt close. Summer is the active growing season.

9.calendar_basis: Summer is the ACTIVE growing season on the cool maritime north coast; there is no summer heat_pause. The season is bounded at the cold/wet winter end instead (cold_pause in the winter months). Absence of heat_pause is intentional and carries this reason (standing principle: absence always carries a reason field).

10.calendar_basis: Summer is the ACTIVE growing season on the cool maritime north coast; there is no summer heat_pause. The season is bounded at the cold/wet winter end instead (cold_pause in the winter months). Absence of heat_pause is intentional and carries this reason (standing principle: absence always carries a reason field).

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: On the California north coast (Monterey County north), summer is actually lettuce's best season, the opposite of hot inland areas. The cool, foggy summers let you grow lettuce from late winter all the way through summer. Plant from February through August. The cold, wet winter, not summer heat, is what ends the season here.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: North-coast calendar is cool-limited and summer-inclusive (Table 13.2: February through August), the inverse of the heat-inverted interior and desert. The cool maritime summer is the active growing season, so there is no summer heat pause; the season is bounded instead by the cold, wet winter. Spring sowing begins once soil is workable and warming; the crop runs through summer and closes as winter sets in. In the mildest coastal microclimates, lettuce can be grown nearly year-round with careful variety selection (UC Marin Master Gardeners), but that is a microclimate refinement, not the regional window. Windows verified against UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2, with UC Marin Master Gardeners corroboration for the maritime cool-season pattern.
ca_north_coast.microclimate_note_seasoned: UC Marin Master Gardeners note that lettuce, generally a cool-season annual, can be grown throughout the year in Marin with advance planning and judicious plant selection. This is a maritime microclimate observation dependent on variety choice, carried here as a refinement; the regional window of record is Table 13.2's February through August. (UC Marin Master Gardeners)

bolting.text_beginner: On the cool north coast, summer is your main lettuce season, not something to avoid. Bolting is less of a constant threat here, but it still happens, often as days lengthen in late spring or during an occasional warm spell. When you see a flower stalk shoot up from the center, harvest the whole plant right away; the leaves stay edible but turn more bitter each day.
bolting.text_seasoned: North-coast summers are mild enough that lettuce runs through them; bolting is driven more by lengthening days and occasional heat spells than by a seasonal heat ramp. Harvest the whole plant at the first flower stalk. Unlike inland regions, you do not pause through summer here.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: On the California south coast (San Luis Obispo County south), lettuce grows across a long, mild cool season. The California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2 gives lettuce in the South Coast as August through April. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program, Table 13.2) The window opens as summer heat eases and runs through the mild winter; San Luis Obispo County Master Gardeners list lettuce among cool-season crops that produce well in the cooler months, with a typical South County last frost around mid-February. (UC Master Gardeners of San Luis Obispo County)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Leaf lettuce on the mild south coast reaches cut size in roughly 45 to 60 days depending on the season within the window; leaf types are at the fast end. Harvest single leaves as soon as they reach a usable size. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The south-coast lettuce season closes as returning spring and summer heat drives bolting. Harvest before sustained warm daytime temperatures. The mild maritime winter rarely limits the crop; heat is the governing constraint. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program, Table 13.2)

May through July is a summer gap on the south coast: lettuce bolts and germinates poorly as temperatures rise. The gap is softer than in the interior or desert (the maritime-influenced south coast stays milder) but still falls outside the Table 13.2 sowing window. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program)

ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: On the California south coast (San Luis Obispo south), lettuce grows across a long, mild cool season from August all the way through April. The winter is gentle enough that you can keep planting through it. Skip the warmest months (roughly May through July), when lettuce bolts and turns bitter. Harvest the spring plantings before summer heat sets in.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: South-coast calendar is summer-excluded and winter-dominant (Table 13.2: August through April), a single long mild-season window. It opens as summer heat eases and closes as returning heat drives bolting. The summer gap (roughly May through July) is softer here than in the interior or desert because the maritime-influenced coast stays milder, but it still falls outside the sowing window. Frost is essentially not a limiting factor (South County last frost around mid-February per SLO County MG); heat governs both ends. Windows verified against UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2, with UC Master Gardeners of San Luis Obispo County corroboration for the mild south-coast cool season.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: In the California low desert (Imperial and Coachella Valleys), lettuce is a fall-through-winter crop; summer is excluded entirely by extreme heat. Sow once summer heat subsides in early fall. The California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2 gives lettuce in the Desert Valleys as September through December. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program, Table 13.2) Imperial County summers run hot and dry (often 90-120 degrees F) with mild winters, and leaf lettuce is a major cool-season crop there. (UC Cooperative Extension, Imperial County)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fall and winter leaf lettuce in the desert matures over roughly 45 to 60 days; cooler winter temperatures and shorter days slow growth relative to warm-season conditions. Harvest single leaves as soon as they reach a usable size. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The desert lettuce season closes as the spring heat ramp returns; lettuce bolts and turns bitter as days lengthen and temperatures climb. Harvest before sustained spring heat. Do not attempt a summer crop in the low desert. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program, Table 13.2)

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: April through August is excluded by extreme desert heat: soil and air well above the bolting threshold cause germination failure and bolting in lettuce. Imperial County summers run 90-120°F. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program; UC Cooperative Extension, Imperial County)

April through August is excluded by extreme desert heat: soil and air well above the bolting threshold cause germination failure and bolting in lettuce. Imperial County summers run 90-120°F. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program; UC Cooperative Extension, Imperial County)

ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: In the California low desert (Imperial and Coachella Valleys), lettuce is a winter crop. Plant from September through December, grow it through the mild winter, and skip summer entirely, when desert heat is far too high for lettuce. Once spring warms up and days get longer, plants bolt (send up a flower stalk) and turn bitter, so harvest before the heat arrives.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: Desert calendar is heat-inverted with a single fall-through-winter window (Table 13.2: September through December sowing). Summer (roughly April through August) is a hard heat exclusion, not a frost gap; Imperial County summers run 90-120°F. The crop finishes ahead of the spring heat ramp, when lengthening days and rising temperatures drive bolting. Frost is not the limiting factor here. Windows verified against UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2, with UC Cooperative Extension Imperial County corroboration for the low-desert climate.

bolting.text_beginner: In the low desert, lettuce is a winter crop, so grow it from September through December and skip summer entirely. As spring warms and days lengthen, plants bolt (send up a flower stalk) and turn bitter fast. When you spot a flower stalk, harvest the whole plant right away, and do not try to carry a crop into the desert summer.
bolting.text_seasoned: Desert lettuce finishes ahead of the spring heat ramp; expect bolting as days lengthen and highs climb. Harvest the whole plant at the first flower stalk. Do not attempt a summer crop in the low desert.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: In the warm arid Southwest (southern New Mexico, West Texas), fall is a primary lettuce season: sow once cresting summer heat subsides in late summer to early fall. Texas A&M AgriLife gives leaf-lettuce fall planting for Texas Region III (USDA zone 8) as approximately September 1. The El Paso County planting calendar places leaf lettuce in the fall garden as the heat breaks. (Texas A&M AgriLife Extension EHT-056; Texas A&M AgriLife Extension El Paso County)

direct_sow.label: secondary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: The arid Southwest's second window is late winter into early spring, before lengthening days and returning heat trigger bolting. NMSU notes lettuce germinates best near 65-70F and bolts when temperatures climb above about 70F with long days; the El Paso County calendar plants leaf lettuce as one of the very earliest spring crops. Sow as soon as the soil is workable and harvest before sustained spring heat. (New Mexico State University Extension Circular 457; Texas A&M AgriLife Extension El Paso County)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fall and winter leaf lettuce in the arid Southwest matures somewhat more slowly than spring plantings as days shorten and cool. NMSU Circular 457-B gives leaf lettuce about 46 days to harvest under favorable conditions; first cuttings of a fall sowing run roughly 50 days. (New Mexico State University Extension Circular 457-B)

harvest_start.label: secondary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Spring leaf lettuce reaches first harvest in roughly 46 days from sowing under the lengthening-day conditions of the arid spring. NMSU Circular 457-B gives leaf lettuce about 46 average days to harvest. (New Mexico State University Extension Circular 457-B)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest closes as returning spring heat and long days trigger bolting, which turns leaves bitter. NMSU: temperatures above about 70F with long days cause lettuce to bolt, and high temperatures cause bitterness. Harvest before sustained warm daytime temperatures. (New Mexico State University Extension Circular 457)
harvest_end.design_note_seasoned: Conservative harvest_end: bolt_threshold_start - 5 days.

8.zone_notes: Arid USDA zone 8 (e.g. Las Cruces NM, El Paso TX): frost-free roughly April through early November. Lettuce runs a spring window (late winter into early spring) and a fall window (late summer into fall), with a hard summer heat pause between them. Light frost is tolerated at the cool winter shoulders; intense summer heat, not frost, governs the season.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer sowing gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: in the arid Southwest, soil and air above the bolting/germination threshold cause germination failure and bolting in lettuce through the May-August heat. NMSU: lettuce bolts above about 70°F with long days and germination is inhibited above about 79°F. (New Mexico State University Extension; Texas A&M AgriLife Extension)

warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: In the warm arid Southwest, lettuce grows in the cooler shoulders of the year, not the summer. Plant a spring crop in late winter to early spring, and a fall crop in late summer once the worst heat breaks. Skip planting through the summer heat, about May through August, when lettuce bolts (sends up a flower stalk) and turns bitter. If you are squeezing in a last spring sowing, get it in by early May; for fall, wait until the heat eases, usually around late August. Light frost in winter is fine; summer heat is the real limit here.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: Region calendar is heat-inverted with two cool-season windows bracketing a summer heat pause: a spring window (sow as soil becomes workable in late winter/early spring, harvest before the spring heat ramp triggers bolting) and a fall window (sow once cresting summer heat subsides in late summer, into fall). The governing constraint is heat, not frost. Texas A&M AgriLife gives leaf lettuce for Texas Region III (USDA zone 8) a fall planting near September 1; the El Paso County calendar runs leaf lettuce as a very-early spring crop and again in fall. NMSU gives leaf lettuce about 46 days to harvest, optimal germination near 65-70°F, and bolting above about 70°F with long days. Frost is a secondary modifier at the cool winter shoulders (arid zone 8 is frost-free roughly April through early November); light frost is tolerated. The summer heat pause (May-August) is a hard exclusion. Windows verified against Texas A&M AgriLife EHT-056 and the El Paso County planting calendar, with NMSU Circular 457/457-B for maturity and bolting biology.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: In the Arizona low desert (Maricopa County ~9b, Yuma), lettuce is a fall-through-winter crop on a single long window; summer is excluded entirely by extreme heat. Sow once summer heat subsides in early-to-mid fall and the soil cools, then continue sowing through the mild winter into late winter. University of Arizona guidance places leaf-lettuce planting across the cool season, and the Yuma calendar gives a September-through-February cool season for lettuce and other non-fruiting greens. Plant after about September 15 once nights and soil cool; avoid sowing while soil is at or above 85 degrees F. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension AZ1005; AZ1615)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fall and winter leaf lettuce in the low desert matures over roughly 45 to 65 days; cooler winter temperatures and shorter days slow growth relative to warm-season conditions. University of Arizona gives leaf lettuce about 30 to 90 days to harvest depending on variety and season. Harvest single leaves as soon as they reach usable size. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension AZ1005)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The low-desert lettuce season closes as the spring heat ramp returns; lettuce bolts and turns bitter as days lengthen and temperatures climb. University of Arizona notes germination is inhibited at high temperatures (thermoinhibition, roughly 77 to 95 degrees F) and the warm season from March onward suits fruiting crops rather than lettuce. Harvest before sustained spring heat; do not attempt a summer crop in the low desert. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension AZ1099; AZ1615)
harvest_end.design_note_seasoned: Conservative harvest_end: bolt_threshold_start - 5 days.

9.zone_notes: Arizona low desert (USDA zone 9b; Maricopa County/Phoenix, Yuma). Frost is occasional and light; lettuce tolerates the rare light frost but not sustained heat. Last spring frost averages around February 15, but winter is mild growing weather for lettuce rather than a pause. The limiting factor is summer heat, not frost: triple-digit highs return in May and persist through August.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: May through August is excluded by extreme low-desert heat: soil and air well above the lettuce thermoinhibition range cause germination failure and bolting. In metro Phoenix the first 100°F day averages early May, and June through August average highs of about 104 to 106°F, far above the 77 to 95°F range that inhibits lettuce germination (University of Arizona AZ1099). April (average high about 85°F) is the spring bolting-close for an established crop rather than a no-sow month, and September is the soil-gated fall sow-resume, so the hard no-activity gap is May through August. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension AZ1099; AZ1615)

low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: In the Arizona low desert (Phoenix, Yuma), lettuce is a winter crop. Plant from about mid-September, once nights cool and the soil is no longer hot, and keep sowing through the mild winter into February. Grow it through the winter and skip summer entirely, when desert heat is far too high for lettuce. As spring warms up and the days get longer, plants bolt (send up a flower stalk) and turn bitter, so harvest before the real heat arrives, usually by April. A rare light winter frost is fine; summer heat is the real limit here.
low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: Low-desert calendar is heat-inverted with a single long fall-through-winter window (sow from about mid-September, once soil drops below the high-temperature germination block, continuing through the mild winter into late February). Summer (May through August) is a hard heat exclusion, not a frost gap. University of Arizona gives a September-through-February cool season for lettuce in the low desert; the Yuma calendar names lettuce as a primary cool-season crop over that span, and Maricopa County guidance runs leaf lettuce across the cool months with a summer break. Germination is inhibited at high soil temperatures (thermoinhibition, roughly 77 to 95°F), which is why the fall sowing waits for the soil to cool rather than for a frost date. The crop finishes ahead of the spring heat ramp, when lengthening days and rising temperatures drive bolting; in metro Phoenix the first 100°F day averages early May. Frost is a minor, occasional modifier at the winter shoulders, not the season boundary. Windows verified against University of Arizona Cooperative Extension AZ1005 (Maricopa County), AZ1615 (Yuma), and AZ1099 (lettuce germination physiology).

bolting.text_beginner: In the Arizona low desert, lettuce is a winter crop, so grow it from about mid-September through February and skip summer entirely. As spring warms and the days lengthen, plants bolt (send up a flower stalk) and turn bitter fast. When you spot a flower stalk, harvest the whole plant right away, and do not try to carry a crop into the desert summer.
bolting.text_seasoned: Low-desert lettuce finishes ahead of the spring heat ramp; expect bolting as days lengthen and highs climb past the mid-80s toward the first 100°F days of early May. Harvest the whole plant at the first flower stalk. Do not attempt a summer crop in the low desert.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: In peninsular Florida (central and south), leaf lettuce is a cool-season crop grown on a single continuous window from fall through late winter. UF/IFAS gives the peninsular planting window as September through February for both central and south Florida. (UF/IFAS VH021, Table 1) Sowing begins once the worst summer heat eases in September and continues through February; the regional calendars list lettuce among the crops to plant from October onward, with February the last month to sow for a late-spring harvest in the deep south. (UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar ENH1191; UF/IFAS Central Florida Gardening Calendar ENH1189)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Leaf lettuce reaches harvest roughly 60 days after sowing under peninsular Florida's cool-season conditions; UF/IFAS lists lettuce at 60-80 days to harvest. (UF/IFAS VH021, Table 1) Fall and early-winter sowings mature into the winter production peak.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Peninsular harvest closes in spring as sustained heat returns and triggers bolting, which turns leaves bitter. The last February sowings finish by roughly April; lettuce is absent from the regional plant calendars from March onward as warm-season crops take over. Harvest before sustained daytime heat. (UF/IFAS VH021, Table 1; UF/IFAS Central Florida Gardening Calendar ENH1189)
harvest_end.design_note_seasoned: Conservative harvest_end: bolt_threshold_start - 5 days.

10.zone_notes: Central Florida (USDA 10 portion, between State Roads 40 and 70). Frost and light freezes are likely in January and February; protect an exposed crop when a freeze is forecast. Lettuce tolerates light frost but not sustained heat.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: peninsular Florida summers run above the bolting threshold, causing germination failure and bolting in lettuce. Lettuce is absent from the central Florida plant calendar from March onward as warm-season crops take over; beds are commonly solarized through summer for fall planting. The sowing window closes in February and the last sowings finish harvest by roughly April, so the no-activity gap is May through August. (UF/IFAS VH021; UF/IFAS Central Florida Gardening Calendar ENH1189)

11.zone_notes: South Florida (USDA 11, below State Road 70). Frost and freezes are rare; the limiting factor is summer heat, not cold. February is the last month to sow for a late-spring harvest. Lettuce tolerates light frost but not sustained heat.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: south Florida summers run above the bolting threshold, ending cool-season production. Lettuce is absent from the south Florida plant calendar from March onward as tropical and heat-tolerant crops take over; beds are commonly solarized through summer for fall planting. The sowing window closes in February and the last sowings finish harvest by roughly April, so the no-activity gap is May through August. (UF/IFAS VH021; UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar ENH1191)

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: In peninsular Florida, lettuce is a cool-season crop, the opposite of up north. Plant from fall through late winter (about September into February), grow it through the mild winter, and skip the summer, when lettuce turns bitter and goes to seed. Winter is your reliable lettuce season here. For the easiest results, aim for the heart of the season, roughly November through January, when temperatures are most consistently cool, rather than the warm edges in early fall or the spring heat ramp.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: Region calendar is heat-inverted and single-window: one continuous cool-season sowing window (September through February per UF/IFAS VH021 Table 1, central and south Florida) bracketed by a summer heat exclusion, not split into two windows the way the more northern Southeast/Gulf zones are. Peak production is winter. The limiting factor is heat-driven bolting, not frost. The two peninsular zones differ mainly in frost exposure: central Florida (zone 10) sees likely January-February freezes that can damage an exposed crop (cover when a freeze is forecast), while south Florida (zone 11) rarely freezes and is heat-limited at both ends. Windows verified against UF/IFAS VH021 (Table 1) with the central (ENH1189) and south (ENH1191) Florida gardening calendars confirming the March warm-crop flip and the September reopening.

The plant_out window in plantings[] is authoritative for sowing dates.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: In Hawaii (tropical, zone 11), leaf lettuce is sown year-round; there is no frost anchor and no seasonal no-sow window for the leaf type. University of Hawaii CTAHR lists green-leaf and red-leaf lettuce as year-round plantings at low elevation and states that leafy and semi-head types can be grown year-round at low elevations, especially under overhead sprinkler irrigation, and that lettuce is grown year-round in most home and community gardens. Heading types are the seasonal exception (cooler months at low elevation, or high elevation) and are not the leaf-lettuce case here. Sow in any month; the heat of summer is managed with a heat-tolerant cultivar and afternoon shade rather than by skipping a season. (University of Hawaii CTAHR RES-164; HGV-2)
direct_sow.from_year_round_note: Anchor from:'year_round' (Decision 3, NA-3g). Frost-independent: zone 11 has no last_frost/first_frost to offset against (zone_frost_data: frost_free_days 365). The resolver keys its 'skip frost resolution, use authored windows as-is' path off this named anchor; resolved_by_zone[11].year_round:true is derivable from it (region anchor = year_round <=> resolved-cell flag set).

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Leaf lettuce in Hawaii reaches cut size in roughly 50 to 60 days from a direct-seeded sowing; CTAHR gives about 50 to 60 days to harvest for direct-seeded Manoa lettuce, the standard low-elevation leaf type, and a few days earlier from transplants. Harvest single leaves or the whole young head as soon as it reaches usable size; harvesting earlier also sidesteps tip-burn and bolting in warm weather. (University of Hawaii CTAHR RES-164)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: There is no season-ending harvest boundary in tropical zone 11: leaf lettuce is sown and harvested continuously through the year. Successive sowings keep a supply coming rather than the crop closing at a frost or a sustained-heat date. In the hottest, longest-day stretch, growth quality dips (tip-burn, faster bolting) but production does not stop; it is managed with cultivar choice and shade. (University of Hawaii CTAHR RES-164; HGV-2)
harvest_end.design_note_seasoned: Year-round cell: harvest_end mirrors the continuous window (from:'year_round', 365) rather than a frost or bolt boundary, because the season does not close. The all-active calendar carries no season_over state by construction.

11.zone_notes: Hawaii tropical (USDA zone 11; frost-free, frost_free_days 365). No frost anchor and no seasonal no-sow window for leaf lettuce. The limiting factor is summer heat quality, not a season boundary: in the hottest months leaf lettuce is grown with a heat-tolerant cultivar (Manoa, Anuenue) and afternoon shade, or moved to higher elevation, rather than paused. Heavy rain can bruise the soft leaves and is the other warm-month management concern.
11.calendar_basis: Leaf lettuce is grown YEAR-ROUND in tropical zone 11; both heat_pause and cold_pause are intentionally absent. There is no winter cold to pause for (frost-free) and no summer no-sow exclusion: University of Hawaii CTAHR lists green-leaf and red-leaf lettuce as year-round plantings at low elevation, and states leafy/semi-head types grow year-round at low elevations and in most home gardens. The summer heat brings a quality dip (tip-burn, faster bolting), managed with a heat-tolerant cultivar and afternoon shade or higher elevation, not a production stop. Absence of both pauses is intentional and carries this reason (standing principle: absence always carries a reason field); the year_round:true flag makes the all-active calendar's intent machine-readable. (University of Hawaii CTAHR RES-164; HGV-2)

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii, leaf lettuce grows year-round, so you can plant a little any month of the year. Pick a heat-tolerant variety such as Manoa or Anuenue, which were bred here to handle the warmth and are slow to bolt. In the hottest, sunniest months, give plants some afternoon shade and keep them well watered, and protect the soft leaves from pounding rain. Lettuce can still bolt (send up a flower stalk and turn bitter) in a hot spell, so harvest leaves young and often. True head lettuce only does well up at higher, cooler elevations; down near the coast, stick with leaf and semi-head types.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: Hawaii's tropical calendar is aseasonal for leaf lettuce: sow and harvest year-round, with no frost anchor and no summer heat pause. University of Hawaii CTAHR lists green-leaf and red-leaf lettuce as year-round plantings at low elevation and notes that leafy and semi-head types grow year-round at low elevations, especially under overhead sprinklers, while heading types are the seasonal, higher-elevation exception. The locally bred 'UH Manoa' (a Green Mignonette selection) and 'Anuenue' are the low-elevation standards; CTAHR describes Manoa as heat-tolerant, slow to bolt, and tip-burn resistant, grown year-round. The hot, long-day months bring a quality dip rather than a production gap: expect faster bolting and more tip-burn, managed with cultivar choice, roughly 40 percent afternoon shade at hot low-elevation sites (per CTAHR shade trials), and a move to higher elevation for head types. Germination falls off above about 81°F, so warm-season sowings benefit from primed seed or a cooler germination spot. Keep soil moisture steady; protect soft-leaved types from heavy rain. Windows verified against University of Hawaii CTAHR RES-164 (Lettuce Production Guidelines for Hawaii), HGV-2 (Lettuce for the Home Garden), and B-91 (Home Gardening in Hawaii).

plantings_provenance.succession_carried_by: succession_policy + resolved_by_zone notes (mirrors northern_tier / fl_peninsula / low_desert_az)
plantings_provenance.window_structure: year_round_continuous (Jan-Dec, all 12 months active) -- NEW SHAPE. UH CTAHR RES-164 Table 1 lists green-leaf and red-leaf lettuce as year-round plantings at low elevation; RES-164 text and HGV-2 confirm leaf/semi-head types grow year-round at low elevation and in home gardens. This is NOT the fl_peninsula/low_desert_az single-window-with-summer-heat-pause shape and NOT the two-window warm_arid/se_gulf shape: there is no summer no-sow exclusion for the leaf type. Decision 1 (Trevor, 2026-06-01, confirmed pauseless): the hot-season quality dip (tip-burn, bolting) is managed with cultivar + shade, not a heat_pause; a heat_pause would encode a no-sow exclusion that directly contradicts the explicit T1 year-round statement. The leaf-vs-head split makes this clean -- the source names this exact type (leaf) as year-round while head types are seasonal.
plantings_provenance.pause_handling: PAUSELESS -- no heat_pause and no cold_pause. Encoded as a POSITIVE declaration per the locked treatment: (1) calendar_basis prose reason on resolved_by_zone[11] (both pauses intentionally absent, CTAHR/elevation/cultivar basis), matching the ca_north_coast no-heat_pause precedent; (2) NET-NEW year_round:true flag on the resolved cell (ca_north_coast still carries detectable cold_pause STATES; Hawaii is the first cell with NO pause signal in calendar[] at all, so the flag makes intent machine-readable). Decision 1 + Refinement A (Trevor, 2026-06-01).
plantings_provenance.year_round_flag_note: year_round:true introduced to the dataset for the first time here (no prior boolean year_round KEY existed; the legacy planting_note value 'year_round' is a separate render hint and is also set on this cell for render consistency with other zone-11 warm crops). Resolver implication: a year_round cell's windows are frost-independent, so the resolver must NOT frost-offset them -- it uses the authored windows as-is, keyed off direct_sow from:'year_round' and/or this flag.
plantings_provenance.declare_one_outcome_invariant: Refinement A (Trevor, 2026-06-01): SCOPED TO THE ALL-ACTIVE CASE. A resolved cell whose calendar[] contains NO pause state (no heat_pause/cold_pause/season_over) MUST carry year_round:true plus its calendar_basis reason. A cell with any pause state in calendar[] is self-declaring and passes without a flag or pause object (passes ca_north_coast: cold_pause STATES + prose, no object; passes future northern_tier). Refinement B: this invariant is SEPARATE from the calendar-model spec Section 6 calendar<->pause-object sync invariant -- Section 6 catches 'calendar disagrees with the pause object it has' (needs an object); this new one catches 'pause entirely omitted, cell silently reads all-active'. Both run; neither absorbs the other.
plantings_provenance.anchor_coherence_note: Decision 3 coherence ask (Trevor, 2026-06-01): region-constant direct_sow uses a distinct from:'year_round' anchor (NOT a frost/bolt anchor overloaded with window_days:365), so the resolver keys 'skip frost resolution, use windows as-is' off a named anchor, and resolved_by_zone[11].year_round:true is derivable from it. plantings_provenance.maturity_basis_note: harvest_start direct_sow_start + 55 days: CTAHR RES-164 gives ~50-60 days direct-seeded for Manoa lettuce (the low-elevation leaf standard), a few days earlier from transplants. Crop-level days_to_maturity [30,45] is the mainland baby/looseleaf figure; the Hawaii cell uses the CTAHR Manoa figure, mirroring how low_desert_az used the AZ-local maturity rather than the crop-level value.
plantings_provenance.zone_calendar_render_note: resolved_by_zone calendar[] shows a steady year-round plant/harvest rhythm (no pause state by construction). The plant_out window in plantings[] (year-round) is authoritative for sowing dates; the alternating render is a legible 'always something to do' depiction, not 12 literal distinct sowing months.
plantings_provenance.tip_override_result: GENUINE ACTION-DIVERGENCE FORK -- bolting tip tip_vntsyt8f forked on hawaii_tropical, CTAHR-sourced. UNLIKE low_desert_az/ca_desert (resolver-mechanics parallel forks of the same skip-summer action) and UNLIKE the portable default ('harvest the whole thing right away at first bolt'): the CTAHR grower action is materially different -- choose a heat-tolerant variety (Manoa/Anuenue), grow YEAR-ROUND, use afternoon shade or higher elevation through the hottest/longest-day months, protect from heavy rain; bolting is managed and slowed, not the trigger for a season-ending harvest and not avoided by a seasonal skip. This is the genuine fork the kickoff flagged Hawaii as the most likely cell to surface (n=1 discipline: authored on evidence of real action divergence, not manufactured). Decision 2 (Trevor, 2026-06-01).

bolting.text_beginner: In Hawaii you grow lettuce year-round, so you do not skip a season; instead you manage the heat. Use a heat-tolerant variety like Manoa or Anuenue, give plants afternoon shade in the hottest, brightest months, and keep them watered. They will still bolt (send up a flower stalk and turn bitter) faster in a warm spell, so harvest leaves young and pick the whole plant once you see a stalk. Up at cooler, higher elevations, bolting is slower and you have more leeway.
bolting.text_seasoned: Hawaii is aseasonal for leaf lettuce: manage bolting with cultivar and microclimate rather than a seasonal pause. Grow heat-tolerant types (UH Manoa, Anuenue), add roughly 40 percent afternoon shade at hot low-elevation sites, and harvest young; bolting and tip-burn accelerate with heat and long days. Harvest the whole plant at the first flower stalk. Higher elevations extend the bolt-free window; head types are reliable only up there.

crops.description_seasoned: One of the fastest, most forgiving crops in the garden, and a strong first-season choice. Sow it directly where it will grow and harvest the outer leaves as cut-and-come-again, taking the oldest first while the center keeps producing. Lettuce is a cool-season crop: it bolts and turns bitter once sustained heat arrives, so the productive window is the cool shoulders of the year. Succession sow small batches every couple of weeks through spring, then again in fall, to keep tender leaves coming rather than harvesting one bed all at once.
crops.description_beginner: One of the fastest and most forgiving crops you can grow, and a great pick for a first garden. Sow the seed right where the plants will grow, then harvest the outer leaves a few at a time, taking the oldest first while the center keeps making new ones. Lettuce is a cool-season crop, which means it grows best in the mild parts of the year: once steady heat arrives it turns bitter and sends up a flower stalk (this is called bolting). To keep tender leaves coming, sow a small batch every couple of weeks in spring, then again in fall, instead of planting one big bed all at once.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Pick the outer leaves whenever they reach usable size, taking the oldest from several plants and leaving the crown to keep growing, or cut the whole plant back to about an inch above the crown for a single larger harvest that regrows. Harvest in the cool of the morning, when leaves are crisp and full of water. The limiting factor is heat: once the central stem begins to elongate (bolting), the plant shifts to flowering, and the leaves turn bitter and tough, so take your fullest harvests before sustained warm weather sets in.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Pick the outer leaves whenever they are big enough to use, taking the oldest ones from several plants and leaving the center to keep growing. Or cut the whole plant back to about an inch above the base for one larger harvest that will grow back. Harvest in the cool of the morning, when the leaves are crisp and full of water. Heat is the limiting factor: once a stalk starts to rise from the center (this is bolting, the plant shifting to making flowers), the leaves turn bitter and tough, so take your biggest harvests before steady warm weather arrives.

crops.name: Orange (Navel)

soil.preferred_texture_seasoned: Deep, well-drained loam to sandy loam
soil.tolerated_texture_seasoned: Sandy and rocky soils with adequate water and feeding; clay only on a raised mound or berm that guarantees drainage
soil.problematic_texture_seasoned: Heavy, poorly drained clay and any site where water stands, which invites Phytophthora foot and root rot
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Oranges care most about good drainage. They like deep soil that drains well and stays slightly acidic, kept evenly moist but never soggy. If water sits around the roots, the tree can get a root rot that is the most common way citrus trees die. If your soil is heavy clay, plant the tree up on a small mound so water drains away, and keep the knobby graft union above the soil. If your soil is alkaline (high-pH), which is common in the desert and inland West, the tree may not get enough iron and zinc, so use a citrus fertilizer that includes those.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Navel oranges demand sharp drainage above all else. They thrive in deep, well-drained loam or sandy loam, slightly acidic, with steady moisture but no waterlogging. The single most important soil decision is drainage: saturated roots lead to Phytophthora foot and root rot, the disease most likely to kill a citrus tree. On heavy clay, plant high on a raised mound or berm so the root crown drains freely, and set the graft union clear of the soil line. High-pH alkaline soils, common in desert and interior-West regions, are workable but tend to lock up iron and zinc, so a micronutrient-inclusive citrus fertilizer and slow acidification help.

ph.note_beginner: Oranges like soil that is slightly acidic, around pH 6 to 7. The main thing to watch for is alkaline (high-pH) soil, common in the desert and inland West, where the tree cannot take up iron and zinc and the leaves turn yellow with green veins. If that happens, use a citrus fertilizer that includes iron and zinc, and over time you can add sulfur to make the soil a little more acidic.
ph.note_seasoned: Navel oranges prefer a slightly acidic soil, roughly pH 6.0 to 7.0, and tolerate a somewhat wider band. The practical issue is high-pH alkaline soil (common in the desert Southwest and interior West), where iron and zinc become chemically unavailable and the tree shows interveinal chlorosis (yellow leaves with green veins) even though the nutrients are present. Correct with chelated micronutrients and a citrus fertilizer that includes them, and acidify the soil gradually with elemental sulfur for a durable fix.

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Citrus are nitrogen-hungry and respond to a feeding rhythm concentrated in the growing season. Feed a mature navel from late winter or early spring through summer in split applications, and stop by late summer so new growth hardens before winter cold. Young trees get smaller, more frequent doses to build the framework. On alkaline soils, use a citrus-formulated fertilizer that includes iron, zinc, and manganese to prevent chlorosis, and water feedings in well. Over-fertilizing pushes excess tender flush that draws aphids, leafminer, and psyllid.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Oranges are hungry for nitrogen and want most of their food during the growing season. Feed a grown tree from late winter or early spring through summer, splitting it into a few doses, and stop by late summer so the new growth toughens up before winter. Feed young trees smaller amounts more often. If your soil is alkaline, use a citrus fertilizer that includes iron and zinc so the leaves do not yellow. Do not overfeed, since extra soft growth attracts pests.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A nitrogen-forward citrus formulation (for example a 2-1-1 ratio) with included micronutrients (iron, zinc, manganese), or a product labeled specifically for citrus and avocado
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: A fertilizer made for citrus (look for one labeled citrus or citrus and avocado); these are higher in nitrogen and include the iron and zinc citrus needs
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: Scale nitrogen to tree age and size: a common guideline is roughly 1 to 1.5 pounds of actual nitrogen per mature tree per year, divided across spring-to-summer applications, with proportionally less for young trees. Follow the product label and local extension rates, which vary by region and soil.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Give more as the tree gets bigger, following the amounts on the citrus fertilizer label and splitting it across spring and summer. A small young tree needs only a little; a big grown tree needs more. When in doubt, follow the package directions for the tree's size.

companions.note_beginner: Keep grass and lawn out from under an orange tree, since grass steals the water and food the tree's shallow roots need. A ring of mulch (kept back from the trunk) is better than grass right up to the tree. There is no real benefit to planting other things close around citrus.
companions.note_seasoned: Keep turf and lawn grasses out of the root zone. Grass competes aggressively for water and nutrients in the top soil layer where citrus feeder roots concentrate, and mowing equipment can damage the trunk. A mulched, grass-free area extending to the canopy dripline is the standard recommendation for all citrus. Low-growing nitrogen fixers like white clover or shallow-rooted ground covers planted outside the trunk flare provide living mulch without root competition. Navel oranges are self-fertile and parthenocarpic, so no pollinizer companion is needed. In fact, nearby citrus with fertile pollen may introduce seeds into otherwise seedless fruit.

pests.name: Asian citrus psyllid
pests.symptoms_seasoned: The psyllid itself is a tiny mottled-brown insect, about an eighth of an inch, that feeds tilted up at a 45-degree angle on new flush, a posture no other citrus pest shares. Its nymphs produce distinctive waxy tubules and curl tender new growth; heavy feeding twists and notches expanding leaves. The insect matters less for its direct damage than for what it carries: it is the vector of Huanglongbing (citrus greening), the most serious citrus disease worldwide. Scout the youngest flush, where it concentrates.
pests.symptoms_beginner: This is a very small brown insect that feeds on the newest leaves, sitting with its back end tilted up in the air, which is a clue it is the psyllid and not something else. The young ones make little waxy white threads and curl the new growth. The real danger is not the bug itself but a deadly disease it spreads (citrus greening), so it is worth taking seriously.
pests.cause_seasoned: Adults lay eggs only on new flush, so populations track flushing cycles and explode in warm weather when trees push tender growth. The pest has spread through most citrus-growing regions of the southern United States; in much of California and the Gulf states it is now established, and any psyllid should be assumed a potential disease carrier.
pests.cause_beginner: The psyllid breeds on fresh new leaves, so it builds up fastest when the tree is putting out tender growth in warm weather. It has spread across the southern states, and any psyllid you find could be carrying the disease.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Buy only certified citrus from a reputable nursery and never move citrus plants or leaves out of a quarantine area, which is the main way the pest and disease jump regions. Inspect each new flush in the warm season. Conserve the natural enemies (a parasitic wasp, Tamarixia, and general predators) that suppress it. Where the disease is present, area-wide psyllid control is the front line.
pests.prevention_beginner: Buy certified citrus from a trusted nursery, and never carry citrus plants or cuttings out of a quarantine zone, because that is how the pest and its disease spread. Check the new leaves often in warm weather. If citrus greening is in your area, follow local guidance on controlling the psyllid.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: On a backyard tree, horticultural oil and insecticidal soap applied to new flush reduce nymphs; thorough coverage of tender growth is key, and repeat as each flush emerges. Do not apply oil above 95°F or to a drought-stressed tree. Most importantly, report suspected psyllids or greening symptoms to your county agricultural office, since this is a regulated pest.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray horticultural oil or insecticidal soap on the new growth to knock back the young psyllids, and repeat each time fresh leaves appear. Hold off on oil when it is hot, above roughly 95°F, or when the tree is short on water, since either condition lets oil burn the leaves. Also report any psyllids or signs of the disease to your local farm advisor or county office, because it is closely tracked.

pests.name: Citrus leafminer
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Silvery, serpentine tunnels winding through new leaves, with a thin dark line of frass down the center of each mine, and leaf margins that curl and pucker around the damage. The larva mines only young, expanding foliage; hardened mature leaves are not attacked. On established trees the injury is cosmetic, but on young trees pushing lots of flush it can slow growth and the curled tissue can shelter other pests.
pests.symptoms_beginner: You will see squiggly silver trails snaking through the new leaves, often with the leaf edge curled up. A tiny caterpillar makes these tunnels inside young leaves only. It looks alarming but rarely hurts an established tree, though it can set back a small young one.
pests.cause_seasoned: A small moth lays eggs on tender new flush, and the larvae mine between the leaf surfaces. Generations cycle quickly in warm weather, so damage peaks on the late-summer and fall flushes rather than the spring growth.
pests.cause_beginner: A tiny moth lays its eggs on the newest leaves, and the larvae tunnel inside them. They breed fast in warm weather, so the worst damage shows up on the late-summer growth.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid pushing excess tender flush with heavy nitrogen or unnecessary summer pruning, since the moth needs young leaves to breed. Tolerate cosmetic mining on bearing trees; resident parasitic wasps usually provide good control if broad-spectrum sprays are avoided.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not over-fertilize or prune a lot in summer, because that creates the tender new leaves the moth needs. On a healthy grown tree, it is best to just live with the trails, since helpful wasps keep it in check.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Chemical control is rarely warranted and broad sprays harm the natural enemies that regulate it. On young trees where protection is justified, horticultural oil on emerging flush deters egg-laying; spinosad is an option but follow heat precautions. Do not spray oil above 95°F. Avoid removing mined leaves, which are still photosynthesizing.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Usually no treatment is needed, and spraying can kill the good bugs that control it. On a small young tree you want to protect, light horticultural oil on the new leaves discourages the moth. Only spray oil in mild conditions, not in high heat or on a thirsty tree, and leave the tunneled leaves on the tree.

pests.name: Scale insects
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Scale appear as fixed, non-moving bumps clustered on twigs, along the leaf midrib, and beneath the leaves. The armored types form firm gray or brown shells that look almost like raised bark, while the softer types are plumper and somewhat glossy. The soft kinds give themselves away by the honeydew they secrete, which leaves foliage tacky and grows a black sooty film, and you will often find ants patrolling the colony for that sugar. Where numbers run high, expect mottled yellow leaves, premature leaf fall, and dieback at the twig tips.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Scale look like little hard or waxy lumps that sit still on twigs and the undersides of leaves, so it is easy to think they are just part of the branch. The softer kinds make the leaves tacky and a sooty black coating grows on that stickiness. Ants are often crawling around them.
pests.cause_seasoned: A mix of armored and soft scale species tap into the tree and feed on its sap. They get the upper hand on trees that are dusty, crowded, or patrolled by ants, because the ants drive away the lady beetles and parasitic wasps that would otherwise thin the colony.
pests.cause_beginner: Scale are little insects that feed on the tree's sap. They get worst when ants are around, since the ants protect them from the helpful bugs that eat scale.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep the tree vigorous and rinse dust off the canopy, and cut off the ants with a sticky trunk band so the resident beneficial insects can do the work. Look any incoming nursery tree over carefully, because scale frequently hitchhikes in on new stock.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep ants from climbing the tree by wrapping a sticky band around the trunk, which lets the good bugs control the scale, and look over any new tree for lumps before planting it.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: A thorough horticultural oil application, narrow-range petroleum or neem, smothers the scale and is the usual home remedy; the key is wetting every surface, especially twig undersides and leaf backs. Skip oil above roughly 95°F or on a tree that is drought-stressed, since heat plus oil scorches foliage. Plan a follow-up as fresh crawlers hatch.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Coat the lumps with horticultural oil, making sure to reach the backs of leaves and the twigs. Save the spray for cooler, well-watered days, never above roughly 95°F or on a drought-stressed tree, or it can scorch the foliage. Spray again later as new ones appear.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of soft-bodied green, black, or brown aphids on the youngest flush and flower buds, with curled, distorted new leaves and a sticky honeydew coating that draws ants and grows sooty mold. Spring and fall flushes are the targets. One species, the brown citrus aphid, is also a vector of citrus tristeza virus, which raises the stakes where that disease is a concern.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Aphids are tiny soft insects, often green or black, that crowd onto the newest leaves and flower buds and make them curl up. They leave a sticky coating that ants love and that grows a black film. They go for the fresh spring and fall growth.
pests.cause_seasoned: Aphids reproduce explosively on tender new growth in mild weather and are tended by ants for their honeydew. Lush, over-fertilized flush is especially attractive, and ant protection lets colonies outrun their natural enemies.
pests.cause_beginner: Aphids multiply very fast on soft new growth in mild weather, and ants protect them. Too much fertilizer makes extra tender leaves that draw them in.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid forcing excessive tender flush with heavy nitrogen. Control ants so lady beetles, lacewings, and parasitic wasps can suppress colonies. A strong jet of water knocks aphids off new growth and is often all that is needed.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not over-fertilize, which makes the soft growth aphids love, and keep ants out so ladybugs and other helpers can eat them. A blast of water from the hose usually clears them off.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: A forceful water spray, insecticidal soap, or horticultural oil controls aphids; cover the undersides of curled leaves. Repeat as needed. Observe oil heat limits (not above 95°F or on stressed trees). Preserve natural enemies by skipping broad-spectrum insecticides.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray them off with water, or use insecticidal soap or horticultural oil, getting under the curled leaves. Keep oil for mild days only, not in high heat or on a stressed, dry tree, and avoid harsh sprays that kill the good bugs.

pests.name: Citrus red mite
pests.symptoms_seasoned: A fine stippling or silvering on leaves and sometimes fruit rind, with tiny dark-red mites and their cast skins visible on leaf surfaces under a hand lens. Heavy populations bronze the foliage and can cause leaf drop. Mites flare in hot, dusty, dry conditions and after broad-spectrum sprays kill their predators, so outbreaks are often a sign the tree is dust-stressed or was over-sprayed.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Look for leaves that turn a dull, speckled, silvery color, sometimes with tiny red dots moving on them (a hand lens helps). Mites get worse when it is hot, dry, and dusty. A lot of them can bronze the leaves and cause some to drop.
pests.cause_seasoned: Citrus red mite thrives in heat and dust and reproduces rapidly on stressed trees. Dusty roadside or driveway trees and trees sprayed with broad-spectrum insecticides (which remove predatory mites) are the most prone to damaging populations.
pests.cause_beginner: These mites love hot, dusty conditions and build up fast on stressed trees. Dusty trees and trees that have been sprayed with strong insecticides (which kill the helpful mites) get the worst of it.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Hose dust off the canopy in hot, dry spells and keep the tree well watered, since vigorous trees tolerate mites better. Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that destroy the predatory mites providing natural control.
pests.prevention_beginner: Rinse dust off the leaves during hot dry weather and keep the tree watered, because a healthy tree handles mites better. Avoid strong insecticides that kill the good mites.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Damage is usually cosmetic and rarely needs treatment. If populations are heavy on a stressed tree, horticultural oil provides control; observe heat limits strictly, as mite outbreaks coincide with the hot weather when oil is riskiest. Do not apply oil above 95°F or to a drought-stressed tree.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Usually the damage is just cosmetic and needs nothing. If there are a lot of mites, horticultural oil works, but timing is tricky: mites peak in hot weather, which is the riskiest time to oil a tree. Only spray when it has cooled off, never on a hot, dry, stressed tree.

pests.name: Katydids and fruit-surface chewers
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Irregular chewed notches on young leaves and, more conspicuously, smooth shallow gouges or healed scars on the rind of developing fruit, where a katydid or similar chewing insect fed when the fruit was tiny. The damage scars over and grows out as the fruit expands, so it is a cosmetic, surface-only blemish that does not reach the flesh of a navel.
pests.symptoms_beginner: You may find ragged bites out of young leaves, or smooth shallow scars on the skin of the fruit where something chewed it when it was small. On a navel this is only skin-deep: the fruit inside is fine, it just looks marked.
pests.cause_seasoned: Katydids and other occasional chewing insects feed on tender foliage and very young fruit in spring and early summer. Populations are usually low and sporadic in a backyard, and the visible scarring is out of proportion to the actual number of insects.
pests.cause_beginner: Katydids and a few other leaf-chewing insects nibble soft leaves and tiny fruit in spring and early summer. There are usually only a few of them, even though the scars look like a lot.
pests.prevention_seasoned: No action is generally needed on a home tree. Healthy trees outgrow the cosmetic injury, and the chewers are kept in check by birds and general predators. Hand-pick if a particular insect is abundant on a small tree.
pests.prevention_beginner: You usually do not need to do anything. The tree grows past the marks, and birds and other predators keep the chewers down. On a small tree you can just pick off any you find by hand.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Treatment is rarely justified for cosmetic rind scarring. Hand-picking handles the occasional katydid. Reserve any spray for genuine defoliation of a young tree, and prefer a targeted product over a broad-spectrum insecticide that would disrupt the citrus natural-enemy complex.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spraying is almost never worth it for marks on the skin. Just pick off the bugs by hand. Only consider a spray if a small tree is being stripped of leaves, and then pick a targeted one rather than a harsh insecticide.

diseases.name: Huanglongbing (citrus greening, HLB)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Blotchy, asymmetric yellowing of leaves that does not mirror across the midrib (distinguishing it from a nutrient deficiency, which is usually symmetric), yellow shoots, and corky, enlarged leaf veins. Fruit are small, lopsided, fail to color fully, stay green at the bottom, and taste bitter and salty; seeds often abort. The tree declines over several years and there is no cure. This is the most destructive citrus disease worldwide.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The classic sign is a leaf that is yellow in a blotchy, uneven pattern, with the yellow on one side of the leaf not matching the other (a nutrient problem is usually even on both sides). Fruit stay small, lopsided, green on the bottom, and taste bad. There is no cure, and the tree slowly dies. It is the worst citrus disease there is.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A bacterium (Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus) that colonizes the tree's vascular system, transmitted by the Asian citrus psyllid as it feeds. Once a tree is infected it cannot be saved, so management is entirely about excluding the psyllid and removing infected trees to protect others.
diseases.cause_beginner: It is caused by bacteria that clog the tree's plumbing, spread by the Asian citrus psyllid when it feeds. Once a tree has it, it cannot be cured, so the whole strategy is keeping the psyllid away and removing sick trees so they do not infect healthy ones.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant only certified disease-free nursery trees, never move citrus out of quarantine areas, and control the psyllid vector aggressively where it is present. Inspect trees regularly and report suspected greening to your county agricultural commissioner, since coordinated removal of infected trees is the only effective area-wide defense.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Buy only certified clean trees, never move citrus out of a quarantine zone, and control the psyllid that spreads it. Check your tree often, and report anything that looks like greening to your local agricultural office, because removing infected trees quickly is what protects everyone's citrus.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure and no organic remedy for an infected tree. Management is prevention and vector control only: protect trees from the psyllid, and remove and properly dispose of confirmed-infected trees promptly so they cannot serve as a reservoir for further spread.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no treatment that saves an infected tree. All you can do is keep the psyllid off your trees and remove any tree that is confirmed infected, so it does not pass the disease to others.

diseases.name: Phytophthora foot rot, root rot, and gummosis
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Watch for gum weeping from the lower trunk and crown (gummosis), and bark at the soil line that turns dark and water-soaked, then later splits and dries as a sunken lesion (foot rot). When the disease works on the feeder roots instead, the tree fades slowly, with leaves yellowing and the canopy thinning out (root rot). The diagnostic clue is foliage that yellows and wilts yet fails to perk up after irrigation, which sets it apart from simple drought, and lesions can climb from the crown onto the lower scaffold limbs.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: This soil water-mold disease shows up as gum oozing low on the trunk, dark mushy bark right at ground level, and a tree that gradually yellows and gets sparse. The big clue: the leaves yellow and wilt but do not bounce back when you water, which means rot rather than thirst.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Phytophthora organisms, which are water molds rather than true fungi, live in the soil and release swimming spores whenever conditions turn wet; those spores splash up onto the trunk or move through saturated ground to the roots. The disease is set up by soggy or poorly draining soil, soil or mulch heaped against the trunk, a graft union buried below grade, and the chronic overwatering that young trees so often receive.
diseases.cause_beginner: It lives in the soil and travels in standing water. It gets going when the ground stays wet, when soil or mulch is mounded up around the trunk, or when the graft union ends up buried. The graft union is that knob low on the trunk, the point where the fruiting variety was joined onto the roots, and it needs to stay above the soil. Watering young trees too much is the usual trigger.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Engineer this one out when you plant, because that is the only reliable defense. Set the tree high on a raised mound so only the topmost roots are covered, hold the graft union well clear of soil and mulch (UF/IFAS recommends keeping it over six inches above grade), grade for fast drainage, hold mulch about a foot off the trunk, and keep irrigation away from the crown. A Phytophthora-tolerant rootstock such as Carrizo, Swingle, or trifoliate stacks on more protection.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Prevention is mostly in the planting. Put the tree up on a small mound, hold the graft union clear of the soil (UF/IFAS says more than six inches above it), make sure water drains off fast, hold mulch a hand's width away from the trunk, and never point water at the base. This is the disease most worth preventing from the start.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Fix the water and drainage problem before anything else, since the tree cannot recover while the roots stay wet. On a fresh trunk lesion you can pare back the dark, dead bark to a rim of healthy green tissue and let the area dry; opening a buried crown to the air sometimes arrests it. Once root rot is advanced on an established tree it is hard to turn around, which is exactly why the planting practices matter so much.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Sort out the drainage or stop the overwatering first, or nothing else will work. For a gummy patch on the trunk, you can gently trim away the dark dead bark down to healthy bark and let it dry out. A serious root case is tough to cure, so getting the planting right up front is what counts.

diseases.name: Citrus canker
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Raised, corky, tan lesions with a water-soaked or oily margin and often a yellow halo, appearing on leaves, twigs, and fruit rind. Unlike many leaf spots, canker lesions erupt through both leaf surfaces and feel rough and raised. Severe infection causes defoliation, twig dieback, and blemished, sometimes dropping fruit. It is a regulated disease in the Gulf states and is far more of a problem in warm, wet, windy climates than in arid ones.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Canker makes raised, rough, tan spots, often ringed with yellow and looking a bit oily at the edges, on leaves, twigs, and the skin of the fruit. The spots come through both sides of the leaf and feel bumpy. Bad cases drop leaves and mark the fruit. It is mostly a problem in warm, wet, windy places like the Gulf Coast.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A bacterium (Xanthomonas citri) that spreads in wind-driven rain and on contaminated tools and hands, entering through natural openings and wounds, including leafminer mines. Warm temperatures, frequent rain, and wind (which wounds tissue and drives the bacteria) make it severe; it is largely absent from dry interior and desert climates.
diseases.cause_beginner: Bacteria spread it through wind-blown rain and on dirty tools and hands. It gets in through tiny wounds, including the tunnels made by leafminers. Warm, rainy, windy weather makes it worse, so it is mainly a humid-climate problem and rarely shows up in dry inland or desert areas.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant certified disease-free stock and choose less-susceptible varieties where canker is established. Avoid working in the canopy when wet, disinfect pruning tools, manage leafminer (whose mines are infection courts) on young trees, and provide good air movement. In regulated areas, follow state guidance, which may include copper programs.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Start with certified clean trees. Do not handle or prune the tree when it is wet, clean your tools between cuts, and keep leafminers under control on young trees since their tunnels let the bacteria in. In areas where canker is a known problem, follow your state's recommendations.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure for an infected tree; management slows spread. Copper-based sprays applied preventively during the wet season reduce new infection and are the standard backyard tool in canker regions. Remove and dispose of heavily infected wood, and disinfect tools between trees. In arid climates, canker is rarely a concern at all.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure, only ways to slow it down. In humid regions, copper sprays during the rainy season help prevent new spots, and you should remove badly infected branches and clean your tools. In dry climates you usually do not need to worry about it.

diseases.name: Greasy spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow mottling on the upper leaf surface that develops into greasy-looking, blister-like brown-to-black lesions on the underside, giving the leaf a translucent, oily appearance. Affected leaves drop prematurely, often in late winter, thinning the canopy. On fruit a fine black speckling (greasy spot rind blotch) can appear. It is primarily a problem in the humid Southeast and Gulf, driven by warm, wet, humid conditions.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Greasy spot makes yellow blotches on top of the leaves and greasy-looking brown or black blisters underneath, so the leaf looks oily. The leaves then fall off early, usually in late winter, thinning out the tree. It is mainly a problem in humid places like Florida and the Gulf.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A fungus (Zasmidium citri-griseum) whose spores develop on decomposing fallen leaves and infect the undersides of leaves during warm, humid, wet weather, with a long latent period before symptoms appear. The decaying leaf litter under the tree is the primary inoculum source, so the disease feeds on its own debris.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus causes it, growing on the old fallen leaves under the tree and then infecting new leaves in warm, humid, wet weather. The dead leaves on the ground are where it comes from, so it keeps itself going through the litter.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rake up and remove fallen leaves under the tree to break the disease cycle, the single most useful cultural step. Promote air movement and avoid prolonged leaf wetness where you can. In dry inland and desert climates the disease is essentially absent and no action is needed.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Rake up and get rid of the fallen leaves under the tree, since that is where the fungus lives, and that one step helps the most. Good airflow helps too. In dry inland or desert areas you will probably never see it.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Sanitation (removing leaf litter) is the core organic control. Where pressure is high in humid regions, a horticultural oil or copper spray timed to early summer reduces infection; oil also helps by suppressing the fungus on leaf surfaces. Observe oil heat limits. Most home trees outside the humid Southeast need no treatment.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Cleaning up the fallen leaves is the main organic fix. In humid regions with a lot of it, a horticultural oil or copper spray in early summer helps, but remember not to use oil on very hot days. Most trees outside the humid Southeast do not need anything.

diseases.name: Sooty mold
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: A black, soot-like film coating leaves, twigs, and fruit that can be rubbed off, leaving the surface beneath unharmed. The mold itself does not infect the tree; it grows on honeydew. Heavy coatings reduce light to the leaf and blemish fruit, but the real problem is the sap-sucking insect producing the honeydew underneath.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Sooty mold is a black, dusty coating on leaves and fruit that wipes off and does not actually hurt the tree underneath. It is a sign that a sticky-honeydew insect (like aphids, scale, or whitefly) is feeding on the tree, because the mold grows on their droppings.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Saprophytic fungi colonize the sugary honeydew excreted by aphids, soft scale, mealybugs, or whitefly. The presence of sooty mold is therefore a symptom of an insect infestation, and ants tending those insects make it worse by protecting them from predators.
diseases.cause_beginner: The black mold grows on the sweet honeydew that sap-sucking insects leave behind. So sooty mold really means you have one of those insects feeding on the tree, and ants often make it worse by protecting them.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Control the underlying honeydew producer (aphids, scale, mealybug, or whitefly) and manage ants, and the mold has nothing to grow on. There is no need to treat the mold itself directly.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Get rid of the insect that is making the honeydew (aphids, scale, and so on) and keep ants out, and the mold will have nothing to grow on. You do not need to treat the mold by itself.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Treat the insect, not the mold: horticultural oil or insecticidal soap on the honeydew producer, plus ant control, resolves both. Existing mold can be hosed or wiped off and will weather away once the honeydew stops. Observe oil heat limits.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Treat the insect causing it with horticultural oil or insecticidal soap, and keep ants away. The mold already there can be rinsed or wiped off and will fade once the stickiness stops. Do not use oil on very hot days.

diseases.name: Brown rot of fruit
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: A firm, leathery, light-brown decay on fruit hanging low in the canopy, usually within a few feet of the ground, often with a pungent odor and, in humid weather, a white mold on the surface. It typically appears on the rind of mature fruit during cool, wet fall and winter weather and can continue to rot fruit in storage. The low position on the tree is the giveaway, since the fungus splashes up from the soil.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Brown rot is a firm tan rot on fruit, almost always on the low-hanging fruit near the ground, often with a strong smell. It shows up on ripe fruit in cool, wet fall and winter weather. The clue is that it is the bottom fruit that rots, because the disease splashes up from the soil.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soil-borne Phytophthora species splash onto low fruit during rain, infecting the rind. Cool, wet weather and fruit or skirt foliage close to the ground create the conditions; the same water molds that cause foot rot are responsible here, attacking fruit instead of trunk.
diseases.cause_beginner: The same kind of soil water-mold that causes trunk rot splashes up onto low fruit when it rains, especially in cool wet weather. Fruit and branches hanging near the ground are the ones that get it.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Skirt-prune the tree so no foliage or fruit hangs within about two feet of the ground, mulch to reduce splash, and harvest low fruit promptly. Good drainage (the same practice that prevents foot rot) reduces the inoculum. In dry-fall climates the disease is uncommon.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Trim the lowest branches so no fruit or leaves hang within about two feet of the ground, add mulch to cut down on splashing, and pick the low fruit early. The same good drainage that prevents trunk rot helps here too. In areas with dry falls it is uncommon.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and dispose of rotted fruit promptly so it does not spread in storage. Where brown rot recurs in wet-winter regions, a copper spray to the lower canopy and fruit before the rainy season is the standard preventive. Skirting and mulching remain the most reliable cultural controls.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick off and throw away any rotted fruit right away so it does not spread to stored fruit. In wet-winter areas where it keeps coming back, a copper spray on the lower fruit before the rains helps. Keeping the low branches trimmed and mulching are the most dependable fixes.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Deep and infrequent.
